Canada uses the word ‘maximum’ on speed signs. Because speed is measured in kilometres instead of miles, the numbers tend to be higher than the US which can be identifiable from afar.

NOTE: The US uses the words ‘speed limit’ on such signs. In addition, speed limits ending with 5 are more common in the US, and the ‘speed limit’ text takes up two lines versus one for ‘maximum’ in Canada.

Canadian road signs tend to be less wordy compared to their US counterparts. Good examples of this are railroad crossing and yield signs. In the US, these usually have the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ and ‘yield’ written on them, whereas in Canada, these signs are typically blank.

The English-speaking parts of Canada use British English spelling (e.g. centre; colour). In addition, Canada mostly uses the metric system. For example, speed is measured in kilometres per hour.

NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the US, where American English spelling and (usually) the imperial system are used. For example, the US measures speed in miles.

Canada uses unique diamond-shaped T-Intersection signs.

NOTE: Canada is the only country in the world where you can find these signs. The US, for example, uses rectangular T-Intersection signs.

Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines. However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.

NOTE: Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US. This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.

Canada has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, especially in rural or remote areas. Generation 2 can be recognized by the big circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

NOTE: Generation 2 is very rare in the US. If you are between Canada and the US, and the location is in Generation 2, you are much more likely to be in Canada.

Generation 3 is significantly more common in Canada than in the US.

In addition, the side mirrors are blurred out differently: While they generally appear as two peaks in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a single peak in the US.

You can sometimes find communal mailboxes in Canada. Personal mailboxes are still very common, though.

Canada Post has a red logo, which sometimes appears on mailboxes.

NOTE: These communal mailboxes are very rare in the US. In addition, the US Postal Service has a blue logo.

The following information applies to both the US and Canada. These tips can be helpful for beginning players who struggle with distinguishing North America from Europe (and other places), especially in low-info rounds.
This style of mailbox, resting on top of a post and with a small flag on the side, is mostly associated with North America.

North America primarily uses wooden utility poles.

Several European countries also primarily use wooden utility poles. However, a concrete pole in particular is mostly associated with Europe.

In addition, the US and Canada use transformers that are large metallic cylinders. This will never be seen in European countries.

This style of insulator, which is raised slightly on top of the utility pole, can be a good clue for the US and Canada. It is not typically found in Europe. It is especially apparent on simple poles with a single insulator.

The United States and Canada will usually have short license plates. Europe usually uses a long license plate which will also have a blue strip on the side.

NOTE: Each province has its own designs. An overview of the specific designs in each province can be seen in step 2.

In the US and Canada, especially at large intersections, long metal bars with stop lights attached to them hang over the street. These bars also commonly have street signs, highway signs, or other signs attached to them.
Thin metal signposts are common. They will typically either have several small holes or have a U profile.
Water towers in towns across the United States and Canada are typically very tall, and sometimes have the name of the town on them.

Both the US and Canada also have Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot. When the car isn’t blurred properly, you will usually see a mirror sticking out on the right side.

Each province has its own unique licence plates, some recognizable from afar even when blurred. Multiple provinces do not require front plates, which can be useful when deciding between provinces.

NOTE: Since 2019, front plates are no longer required in New Brunswick. However, you should still expect to see them in older coverage. As well, all commercial vehicles in Newfoundland and Labrador are required to use front plates, and so it is possible to see them on vans and pickup trucks.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

French is the majority language in Québec and parts of New Brunswick.

NOTE: At the federal level, French has official status alongside English, so you can sometimes find bilingual signs in other parts of Canada. In addition, French is also spoken in several communities in Nova Scotia, Ontario and Manitoba.

Each province has their own highway shields with unique designs.

The green Trans-Canada Highway shield, shown in the top right of the image, can be found in all 10 provinces.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Each province has its own unique kilometre markers that vary slightly.

Notably, Ontario KM markers have a white square at the bottom, which is unique to the province.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Some provinces have unique speed signs.

Ontario speed limit signs may have a black section on the bottom with the words ‘km/h’ or ‘begins’ written in white.

British Columbian signs also include the ‘km/h’ but lack the black section.

Québec can sometimes have French on their speed limit signs.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

NOTE: Some Alberta bollards have a yellow band between the two black bands, instead of a white one. Blue bands can also rarely be seen, particularly in and around Calgary, while green bands are rarely seen in and around Edmonton.

Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.

Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba.

NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

British Columbia has black-and-white bollards with a thin, slightly curved shape. It is most commonly found on Vancouver Island, but can be found all throughout the province.

NOTE: They can look superficially similar to the Alberta bollard. However, the thin shape and the wider spacing of the two black bands should help you tell them apart.
Québec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

You will often find these yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts in Québec.

In Québec City these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small.

NOTE: Sometimes the markers will have different colours. Beware that Edmundston, in New Brunswick, uses these too.

You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary.

NOTE: These can be rarely found on urban divided highways in New Brunswick.
You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.

The Northwest Territories has a black and white bollard with a cylindrical shape and two thick, black bands.

NOTE: It looks very similar to the Alberta bollard. However, the Alberta bollard has thinner black bands.
The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.
Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.

Insulators facing towards or away from the road are mostly found in Québec, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island. Other provinces tend to have their insulators facing the same direction as the road.

NOTE: This is most trustworthy when the pole is not at an intersection or driveway.

These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.
Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.

Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in Manitoba.
Poles with two hanging insulators are common in Manitoba.
Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.
Poles on Prince Edward Island usually feature a small white sticker.
Québec T-Intersection signs do not feature the chequerboard pattern.
Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.

Road signs in British Columbia can have green backsides.

NOTE: Green backsides are also somewhat common on Prince Edward Island.
Signs in British Columbia are sometimes hung down from these unique signposts.
You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.
Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these white triangles. The number can vary.
Stop signs with the word ‘Arrêt’ are unique to Québec.

Stop signs with both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are most commonly found in New Brunswick.

NOTE: Such stop signs can rarely be found in other provinces.

Like the stop signs, street signs in New Brunswick are also bilingual.

Though unlike the stop signs, bilingual street signs are found in other French minority areas of Canada.

Rural roads in Alberta are numbered sequentially. This makes it easy to figure out your exact location using just a road sign.

  • Township roads (Twp Rd) run east to west. Their numbers increase the more north you go.
  • Range roads (Rge Rd) run north to south. Their numbers increase the more west you go. These numbers reset a couple of times.

This infographic shows which numbers are found where. You need to multiply the numbers on the grid by 10 to get the road numbers. For example, the junction in the image example is found just north of Red Deer.

NOTE: Similarly named roads can also sometimes be seen in Saskatchewan, however they are more common in Alberta.

Rural roads in Manitoba are organised in a grid and referred to only by their number and cardinal direction.

  • Roads ending in N run east to west. Their numbers increase by one for every mile north of the US border.
  • Roads with E or W run north to south. They tell you their position relative to the principal meridian, located just west of Winnipeg.

For instance, this image was taken 105 miles north of the US border and 147 miles west of the principal meridian.
British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.
This guardrail, with small poles connected by three or four metal wires, can rarely be found on major highways in Alberta.
In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.
In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.
Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.
You can spot these wooden boxes holding up signs in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Within Eastern Canada, double yellow lines are most common in Nova Scotia, followed by Québec and Prince Edward Island. Ontario prefers single yellow lines for this purpose, but will occasionally use them.

_For some empirical research, please see this document._
You can sometimes find white dashes between the yellow centre lines in Saskatchewan.
Rumble strips in the centre of the road (generally over the roadlines) are most common in Alberta and British Columbia.

Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones.

Québec, on the other hand, has unique orange and white striped traffic cones.

Québec is the only Canadian province that uses red and white chevrons.

NOTE: The rest of Canada uses the classic yellow and black chevrons.
New Brunswick and Nova Scotia commonly use lampheads with a rectangular shape.

Lamp arms on utility poles in Nova Scotia are usually curved and much shorter than in the rest of Canada.

NOTE: Short lamp arms may occasionally be found in other parts of Canada.

Bins made of wood planks can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. These are most commonly octagonal, however they can have other shapes.

NOTE: Although they are most common in Newfoundland, they can also sometimes be seen in other provinces, such as New Brunswick.
Western Canada is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta, and parts of Yukon. Outside these provinces, large mountains are rare to non-existent in Canada.

Yukon has a very northern, boreal landscape that is mostly hilly, sometimes with large mountains in the distance. Coniferous trees line the roads and the further north you go, the thinner and shorter the trees get. Older Generation 2 coverage is common in this region.

The landscape in the interior of southern British Columbia, mostly centred around the towns of Kamloops and Kelowna, has a distinct look. It is generally hilly and a little more arid than the rest of BC. The vegetation consists of sprawling brown grasslands, and pine tree forests on the hillsides.

The Great Plains are mostly flat, with some rolling hills. There is a lot of agriculture, very few trees, and it is very sparsely populated. The landscape gets drier the further south-southwest you go, with the driest parts near the border with the US state of Montana.

Canola is grown in the central southern prairies, and it can be found almost nowhere else in Canada. It is visually similar to a field of bright yellow flowers.

NOTE: Canola is also very common in the US state of North Dakota.

The region around Rouyn-Noranda in northwestern Québec can mainly be characterised by the north-south grid, along with the slightly hilly landscape featuring many agricultural fields nestled between the forests, which have many shorter trees as well as thin birches.

Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys, which means that the province can have a barren hilly landscape; much more so than the rest of the Canadian Great Plains, which tends to be really flat.

NOTE: Some of this hilliness extends into southern Alberta and Manitoba.

Aspen trees are common in the forested parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They are recognizable by their white, birch-like trunks. In most seasons, they have regular green leaves, but in fall coverage, they turn a characteristic bright yellow colour.
The Canadian Shield extends through the eastern part of Canada. Therefore, you will commonly see exposed rocks on street view in the highlighted area.

The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is the most densely populated part of Canada. It is mostly flat and green, with a patchwork of agriculture and occasional forest cover.

NOTE: This area can look similar to the Great Lakes region in the US.

Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint to it. Potato farming is also very common on PEI.

NOTE: This type of soil can occasionally be seen in certain areas of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

The Balsam Fir is a very common species of tree found in Newfoundland. It has a Christmas tree-like appearance.

NOTE: While most commonly found in Newfoundland, the Balsam Fir can also grow in other parts of Eastern Canada and the US. For an overview, see this map.

Canadian phone numbers start with a three-digit area code. Both landlines and mobile phones use the same area codes.

NOTE: Canadian phone numbers are formatted XXX XXX XXXX, with the area code being the first three digits. It is fairly common to see 7-digit numbers with the area code omitted.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Provincial flags appear decently often. The Fleurdelisé of Québec in particular is very common.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Acadia is a French-speaking cultural region in the Canadian Maritimes without clearly defined borders. It is usually understood to at least include north and east New Brunswick, with some isolated communities in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

It has its own flag, which is a French-style tricolour with a yellow star in the blue band. It can be seen either flown or painted on poles in this region.
These flat, yellow bollards can be found on the Trans-Canada highway in New Brunswick.

The Dempster Highway (road numbers 5 and 8) connects the Klondike Highway (road number 2) in Yukon with the remote town of Inuvik in the Northwest Territories.

It is very recognizable: it is an unpaved road with Generation 2 coverage, dark brown soil, and a tundra landscape with short trees. It is mostly hilly and mountainous, but the section between Fort McPherson and Inuvik is flat. Closer to Inuvik, the weather gets cloudy.
The Top of the World Highway west of Dawson City in Yukon has overcast Generation 2 coverage and is located mostly high up in the mountains, making it recognizable.
A group of motorcyclists can be seen in front of the Google car on this stretch of Highway 1 near Beaver Creek in Yukon.
The AB-93 highway through Banff and Jasper National Park features distinct, gradual, and steep mountains with a sharp peak on either side of the road. Tall, somewhat thin trees can also be seen.
The area near Drumheller, Alberta has distinct canyon-like treeless rock formations that comprise the landscape.

The Trans-Labrador Highway (road numbers 500 and 510) is a recognizable road, covered by Generation 4, mostly during sunny weather conditions. Thin pine trees line the side of the road, and it has a remote, cold, and northern feel. On many parts of the road, the sun is low in the sky. In addition, when the car drives past the city of Happy Valley-Goose Bay, it is common to see snow on the ground.
QC-167 and QC-113 are covered in Gen 3 and identifiable for their overcast autumn coverage, often with snow on the ground. In addition, a smudge can be seen on this road.
The inland roads of the Gaspé Peninsula feature densely forested mountainous terrain. It is particularly common to encounter overcast coverage in this region.
The Cape Breton Highlands in northeastern Nova Scotia have an unusual amount of elevation for Eastern Canadian standards. It is very forested, with a mix of broad-leaf trees and pine trees.

Route 430 on Newfoundland runs in a roughly south-southwest to north-northeast direction, with the road lines slightly washed out. It is located in a remote and sparsely populated part of the island. On many sections of the road, the coast is visible to your west. To your east, you will usually see low balsam fir forests, and occasionally an imposing wall of mountains in the far distance.

Iqaluit is the capital of Nunavut, meaning it is more urban, and built up compared to other Nunavut settlements. The city features bilingual turquoise street signs. Speed limit signs are also uniquely bilingual. And on the outskirts of the city, these unique road markers can be seen.

The remote town of Churchill in northern Manitoba features a trekker with a distinct thin antenna visible on the front right side of the car. The town also has unique street signs.

NOTE: This coverage is also seen in the surrounding area.

This unique Google car and dark-coloured soil is found in Tulita, NWT. The car will most often look like this, but can also be fully blurred with just the antenna visible, or with the hood of the car visible.

Sanikiluaq is a remote town situated in Hudson Bay. This snowy town was covered by a snowmobile whose driver wore a dark brown coat.

NOTE: Snowmobile coverage can be found outside the town on the ice-covered sea, where the driver is not visible.

Inukjuak is a town in northern Québec. This town can be recognized by the snowmobile that is visible through the blur.

NOTE: In Sanikiluaq, the other town with snowmobile coverage, you will always see the driver.
Grise Fiord is the northernmost covered town in Canada. It can easily be recognized by these unique mountains and the ice floes on the coast.
The northern town of Resolute can be recognized by the barren landscape with visible patches of snow.
Cambridge Bay is the only Nunavut settlement to have Generation 2 trekker coverage.
The town of Qikiqtarjuaq features distinct mountains, and red tinted soil.
Kangiqsualujjuaq is a town in northern Québec, surrounded by green rocky hills, with trees visible in the distance.

Nain is a small town on the Northeastern coast of Labrador. The town features colourful wooden houses, and trees in and around the town. To the north, a big hill is usually visible. And to the south, rocky cliffs can be seen on the other side of the bay. Additionally, kids can sometimes be seen walking beside the trekker.
Red Bay is a town on the southern coast of Labrador, and as such, the coast is always visible. It features slightly red soil, and most of the houses are painted white.

The northernmost Google Street View coverage in the world is a trekker on Ellesmere Island in northern Nunavut. It shows a glacier in a rocky, desolate landscape that is devoid of any vegetation.

NOTE: This coverage is sometimes used in maps to improve and standardise the scoring range. As a result, you might encounter this trekker in competitive maps like ACW, despite it not being pinpointable.

lm.name: Cape Breton National Park
lm.note: The Cape Breton Highlands in northeastern Nova Scotia have an unusual amount of elevation for Eastern Canadian standards. It is very forested, with a mix of broad-leaf trees and pine trees.

lm.name: Drumheller Canyons
lm.note: The area near Drumheller, Alberta has distinct canyon-like treeless rock formations that comprise the landscape.

lm.name: Gaspé Peninsula
lm.note: The inland roads of the Gaspé Peninsula feature densely forested mountainous terrain. It is particularly common to encounter overcast coverage in this region.

lm.name: Great Plains
lm.note: The Great Plains are mostly flat, with some rolling hills. There is a lot of agriculture, very few trees, and it is very sparsely populated. The landscape gets drier the further south-southwest you go, with the driest parts near the border with the US state of Montana.

lm.name: Max Max North Coverage
lm.note:
The northernmost Google Street View coverage in the world is a trekker on Ellesmere Island in northern Nunavut. It shows a glacier in a rocky, desolate landscape that is devoid of any vegetation.

NOTE: This coverage is sometimes used in maps to improve and standardise the scoring range. As a result, you might encounter this trekker in competitive maps like ACW, despite it not being pinpointable.

lm.name: Québec City Windsor Corridor
lm.note:
The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is the most densely populated part of Canada. It is mostly flat and green, with a patchwork of agriculture and occasional forest cover.

NOTE: This area can look similar to the Great Lakes region in the US.

lm.name: South Saskatchewan Hills
lm.note:
Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys, which means that the province can have a barren hilly landscape; much more so than the rest of the Canadian Great Plains, which tends to be really flat.

NOTE: Some of this hilliness extends into southern Alberta and Manitoba.

lm.name: Southern British Columbia
lm.note: The landscape in the interior of southern British Columbia, mostly centred around the towns of Kamloops and Kelowna, has a distinct look. It is generally hilly and a little more arid than the rest of BC, The vegetation consists of sprawling brown grasslands, and pine tree forests on the hillsides.

lm.name: Western Mountains
lm.note: Western Canada is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta, and parts of Yukon. Outside these provinces, large mountains are rare to non-existent in Canada.

lm.name: Yukon
lm.note: Yukon has a very northern, boreal landscape that is mostly hilly, sometimes with large mountains in the distance. Coniferous trees line the roads and the further north you go, the thinner and shorter the trees get. While this region recently got a lot of new Generation 4, older Generation 2 coverage is still very common.

lm.name: Central rumble strips
lm.note:
Within the Prairies, rumble strips on the centre line are only found in Alberta.

Note: Rumble strips on the outer lines can also be found in other provinces.

lm.name: Extreme Southwest
lm.note: In the extreme Southwest of Alberta you will find slightly rolling, grassy fields with the Southern Rockies visible to the West.

lm.name: Generic guardrail
lm.note: Alberta tends to use more generic guardrails than any other Prairies province. Sask and Manitoba have way less guardrails in general and those are often of an unconventional type.

lm.name: Horizontal sticker
lm.note: Even though pole stickers are not the most reliable in the Prairies, horizontal metal stickers are common in Alberta. They are usually grey and can be either blank or have small numbers on them. Yellow variants exist too.

lm.name: Isolated hills
lm.note:
From certain roads in Far Southern Alberta isolated hills can be seen over the border in Montana.

Note: They are best visible from Provincial Highways 501 (Gen 4), 500 (Gen 2) and 880 (Gen 2).

lm.name: Missing insulator poletop
lm.note:
Alberta has a poletop that is similar to the one found in Manitoba, but with a missing insulator on the bottom crossbar.

Note: The poletop is found in abundance around Edmonton.

lm.name: Northern > poletop
lm.note:
A very distinct ">" shaped poletop can be found on the roads of Northern Alberta.

Note: It is especially common on the MacKenzie Highway (Hwy 35) between High Level and Warrenzie, as well as West of High Level on Hwy 58.

lm.name: Peace River street sign
lm.note:
While most rural street signs in Alberta are blue, green signs can be found concentrated around the Peace River Area in the Northwest.

Note: In the rest of the Prairies, green is the standard rural street sign colour. Larger cities in Alberta often use green as well.

lm.name: Standard Canadian lamp
lm.note:
Lamps in Alberta follow the standard Canadian design: no curve, no support bar.

To differentiate from other Prairies:

  • Sask lamps often have a curve and a support bar
  • Manitoba can use the same type, or an excessively long, supported lamp arm.

lm.name: Standard poletop
lm.note: The standard Alberta poletop looks fairly generic: it has a medium-lenght crossbar with 3 vertical insulators each connected to its own wire.

lm.name: Atlantic Canada  - Blue house number
lm.note:
Rural house numbers in Nova Scotia tend to be blue with white lettering.

Note: This style is also common in New Brunswick and PEI, only less consistently. Make sure to look for other clues first!

lm.name: Atlantic Canada  - Clapboard architecture
lm.note:
While houses made of white siding wood are generally common throughout rural Canada, with some practice the iconic Atlantic Coast clapboard houses can be recognised. Influenced by British and New England architecture, these houses feature steep dark grey gable roofs, multiple stories, simple symmetrical facades and often an elaborate entryway.

Note: This style gets more common the closer you get to the Atlantic coastline. Look for the coastal village setting!

lm.name: Atlantic Canada  - Colourful houses
lm.note: Aside from the white wooden houses, Eastern Canada also has a lot of colourful houses. They are especially common in fishing villages in the Maritimes, in coastal Québec as well as some bigger towns such as downtown St John's (NL) and Lunenburg (NS).

lm.name: Atlantic Canada  - Square lamp
lm.note:
Square lamp heads are common in both New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. To differentiate, you can look at the lamp arm: NB mostly uses long, straight ones while NS prefers short and curved. PEI's lamps are usually similar to the ones in Nova Scotia, although I have also seen the New Brunswick style there.

Note: Don't rely on the blue bumps on the top of the lamps being only in NS as NB also has them!

lm.name: 2+1 poletop
lm.note:
Poletops with asymmetrical insulators, arranged in a 2+1 pattern are common in British Columbia.

Note: They don't alternate like the ones in Saskatchewan.

lm.name: Darker poles
lm.note: Poles in Western Canada - especially in BC - tend to be darker and have fewer knots than poles in the East. In BC, it is common to find poles with a reddish tint.

lm.name: Double crossbeam
lm.note: Double crossbeams can often be found on utility poles in British Columbia.

lm.name: Fake Ontario poletop
lm.note:
Occasionally, you might find poletops in BC that resemble the classic Ontario poletops.

To avoid the bait, here are some details to look for:

  • ON never uses generic mushroom insulators on a V-poletop
  • completely flat or strangely long "U" attachments are BC only
  • BC's insulators usually have longer and thinner ribs than ON.

...but the best is just to look at the landscape first.

lm.name: Flat land
lm.note:
British Columbia has 3 main areas with flat land:

  • in the Southwestern lowlands nearby Vancouver (Fraser River delta)
  • in the Centre, nearby Prince George (Fraser and Nachako River valleys)
  • in the Northeast, from Fort St John and northwards (Peace River area).

lm.name: Hydro box
lm.note:
In British Columbia, large green electric boxes often feature the name of the local electricity distributor, "BC Hydro", or simply "Hydro".

Note: Unfortunately, large green boxes are quite rare in BC. (You might find 1 or 2 per town.)

lm.name: Longer secondary crossarm
lm.note: In British Columbia, secondary crossarms on utility poles are usually longer than the top ones.

lm.name: Metal circles
lm.note: BC would often have 1 to 5 small metal circles at the lower part of her utility poles.

lm.name: Metal flare
lm.note: Metal flares at the bottom of the utility pole are typical for British Columbia.

lm.name: Metal pole rectangle
lm.note: Small yellow or grey metal rectangles are found on most utility poles in BC.

lm.name: Northeastern landscape
lm.note: The Northeastern region of British Columbia is known for its rolling hills and vast boreal forests with white aspen trees. Aside for a short section of the BC-97 going through the Northern Rockies, there is no coverage with tall mountains here.

lm.name: Northwestern landscape
lm.note:
Northwestern British Columbia can be recongised by its large, often snow-capped mountains, tall but thin evergreens, low green bushes, boreal mosses and flowers. The roads here still have Gen 2 coverage, adding to the remote, Alpine vibes.

Note: The extreme Northwest near the Yukon border has ominously gray, cloudy weather.

lm.name: Redcedar needles
lm.note:
On Vancouver Island and the nearby humid coastal areas of Southwestern British Columbia, you can often see a reddish carpet of fallen pine needles covering the sides of the road. This is caused by the Western redcedar shedding its needles, with some contribution from Douglas firs.

Note: Redcedar needles can also be found in the temperate rainforest areas of Oregon and Washington in the US. Small, isolated pockets might also occur further inland in BC, but they are less obvious.

lm.name: Standard poletop
lm.note:
The most common poletop in British Columbia is a simple T-poletop with 3 (usually white) mushroom insulators. The middle one is mounted higher than the other 2.

Note: This poletop also exists with large UFO-shaped insulators in BC.

lm.name: Stoplights
lm.note:
Stoplights in British Columbia are always vertical and yellow. The middle part can be yellow (eg. Vancouver City, Kamloops) or black.

Note: Middle part colours can be quite inconsistent, even within the same town.

lm.name: Vancouver Island vibes
lm.note:
Parts of Vancouver Island is covered by a temperate rainforest. Trees are even taller and denser here than in most other parts of the province.

Note: Gen 3 is still quite common on Vancouver Island.

lm.name: Yellow fire hydrants
lm.note:
Within British Columbia, you can use fire hydrant body colours for further regionguessing. Yellow body hydrants are found in the Central regions of the province, from the Peace River area through the Okanagan valley, down to the US border.

The peripheries of the province use red body hydrants.

lm.name: British Columbia / Alberta  - Rockies
lm.note: To distinguish the Canadian Rockies from the Coast Mountains and other ranges in Western Canada, you can look for sharp, treeless mountaintops and exposed rocks of a lighter colour.

lm.name: British Columbia / Alberta  - Yellow curbs
lm.note:
Yellow curbs can often be seen in British Columbia and Alberta.

Note: Other provinces can also have them, so only use this meta if you can't find anything better.

lm.name: British Columbia / Québec  - "L" poletop
lm.note:
Reverse L-shaped poletops are common in British Columbia and Québec - especially on the Gaspé-peninsula.

Note: The insulators and the colour of the wood are different in the two provinces.

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - A frame pole
lm.note:
If you see an A-frame pole, New Brunswick is the most likely option followed by Newfoundland & Labrador, Québec and Ontario.

Note: While these poles are generally rare in Canada, they can occasionally show up in any part of the country. Look for other clues first!

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - Eastern white pine
lm.note:
The Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) can be recognised by its oval crown, long needles and horizontal, tiered branches. It is useful for getting the Eastern half of the country in ultra-rural rounds.

Tip: If you see it in very large quantities, you are probably further South within its range. (Eg: somewhere close to the Great Lakes, the New England border or Southern Nova Scotia).

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - Isolated UFO insulator
lm.note:
Isolated stubby ribbed insulators (UFO shape) can be found in Ontario, Québec and Newfoundland & Labrador.

Note: Some regions have more of them, such as the extreme Southwest in Ontario or the far East of Québec.

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - Lighter poles
lm.note: Utility poles in Eastern Canada (The Maritimes and Québec - especially the East) are made of a lighter coloured wood and have more visible knots on them.

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - Maple trees
lm.note:
Canada is home to 10 native maple species, including the iconic Sugar Maple (Acer saccharum) and the Red Maple (Acer rubrum). These trees can be recognised by their large round crowns and lobed leaves - just like the one on the Canadian flag. On fall coverage, their brilliant orange-red foliage can be seen from far away. You can find a lot of these trees in the St. Lawrence Lowlands and the Maritimes.

Note: Maples are useful for excluding the Northern parts of Ontario and Québec, as well as NL.

lm.name: Eastern Canada  - Tiny hanging lamp
lm.note:
An old-timey looking lamp hanging from a very short, triangle shaped arm is unique to the Maritime Provinces. It is by far the most common in Nova Scotia.

Note: While I haven't seen this design on Newfoundland Island, Labrador seems to like it a lot. More research needs to be done on PEI.

lm.name: Gravel ditch
lm.note: A thick strip of light coloured gravel on the sides of the road is a good clue for Manitoba. On many roads white outer lines are entirely replaced by gravel ditches.

lm.name: Hanging insulator poletop
lm.note:
Trident poletops with 2 hanging insulators are pretty much unique to Manitoba. They exist with or without a secondary crossbar.

Note: This poletop is way more common on the Southern plains of Manitoba than further North.

lm.name: Insulator patterns
lm.note:
Manitoba's wooden poles can have the same 2+1 arrangement as Saskatchewan's, but they will not alternate consistently. It is possible to find poles with different insulator patterns standing right next to each other.

Note: Manny's crossbars are also shorter and the insulators are often smaller or darker than Sask's.

lm.name: Keyhole sticker
lm.note: Even though rural pole stickers are quite unreliable on the Prairies, Manitoba's poles often have a distinct metal sticker shaped like a "keyhole". (A circle with a trapezoid underneath).

lm.name: Long supported lamp arm
lm.note:
An excessively long, supported lamp arm will most likely put you in Manitoba.

Note: Most of Manitoba's lamp arms will be the standard Canadian style though.

lm.name: October snow
lm.note: East of Winnipeg, nearby the border with Ontario 2 roads with patchy snow coverage can be found (MB 307 and the Eastern part of Hwy 44). The images were taken in October (copyright is 2019) with a Gen 3 camera, so there is a distinct Autumnal feel to them. The landscape is hilly and forested.

lm.name: Side wire attachment
lm.note: Wires attached to the side of the pole are more common in Manitoba than in the other Prairies provinces.

lm.name: Sign clasp
lm.note: Rural towns in Manitoba still use metal sign clasps specific to the province.

lm.name: Trident poletop
lm.note:
Manitoba's most iconic poletop is a long trident with long insulators, often with a secondary crossbar underneath.

Note: It also exists with alternative insulator types - what matters is the long trident shape.

lm.name: Typical landscape
lm.note: The typical Manitoban landscape features a mix of gently rolling hills and flat agricultural fields with patches of aspen parks in between. The open Prairie-like parts are in the South / Southwest, then you see a gradual transition into the boreal pine forest as you move Northeast.

lm.name: 1 bolt pole
lm.note: Many insulators in New Brunswick are fixed with only 1 bolt to the pole. The rest of Canada uses 2.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note:
New Brunswick has a variety of rectangular bollards, usually found at guardrail-endings. Most common colours: green, pink and yellow (famously on the Trans-Canada Highway).

Note: Blocky-looking wooden bollards with a red or green reflector are also possible to get.

lm.name: Double insulator pole
lm.note:
Poles with two insulators on top are more common in New Brunswick than in any other province.

Note: Newfoundland and Labrador seems to have a lot of these poles too.

lm.name: Forested hills
lm.note: The typical New Brunswick landscape consists of lush rolling hills covered in evergreens, such as pines and spruces.

lm.name: Generic guardrail
lm.note: New Brunswick uses pretty generic looking guardrails. This is useful for differentiating between NB and the other Maritimes (especially NS and NL) that use more unique guardrail types.

lm.name: Green sticker
lm.note:
Directional signs and poles at larger intersections in New Brunswick often have a green sticker with white lettering on the signpost.

Note: Many of these green stickers have "New Brunswick" written on the top alongside a logo, but you need to go close to be able to read it.

lm.name: Language regions
lm.note: You can subdivide New Brunswick by how much French language you can see around. The Northern counties and the East coast are Acadian territory where most text will be bilingual (or French only). In the Central and Southern counties the usage of French will be limited to street signs and official buildings.

lm.name: Long straight lamp
lm.note:
New Brunswick lamps can be recognised by their length and straightness. They usually feature square lamps with a blue photocell on top.

Note: Lamp arms in Nova Scotia are shorter and more curved.

lm.name: No roadlines coverage
lm.note: New Brunswick has a lot of coverage on rural asphalt roads without any roadlines.

lm.name: Yellow pole sticker
lm.note: Yellow horizontal pole stickers with black numbers are common in New Brunswick. There can be one or more on the same utility pole.

lm.name: New Brunswick / Nova Scotia  - Curved sign border
lm.note:
Rural road signs with a white, curved border can be found in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

Note: This is a pretty standard design for directional signs in all of Canada, so make sure it says a road name to narrow it down to NS or NB!

lm.name: New Brunswick / Nova Scotia  - Stoplight styles
lm.note:
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick use similar stoplight designs, but NS is more likely to use solid yellow ones, while NB has more solid black ones, or yellow ones with a black middle part.

Note: The city of Amherst (NS) close to the border with NB uses solid black stoplights.

lm.name: Burin dryness
lm.note:
The Burin Peninsula in the far South of Newfoundland has a distinctly dry and barren landscape.

Note: The general South of Newfoundland tends to be dryer and have fewer trees than the rest of it.

lm.name: Eastern insulator
lm.note:
Insulators whose top rib is larger than the bottom one are the most common on the Eastern parts of Newfoundland. The Avalon Peninsula seems to love them a lot.

Note: There is another insulator type on the island with 2 equally small ribs and a larger top one. This is not specific to the East!

lm.name: Eastern poletop
lm.note:
A poletop with 2 horizontal insulators pointing in opposite directions and one vertical insulator on top is commonly found on the Eastern part of Newfoundland.

Note: If you see this poletop in a cloudy October landscape with a 2019 copyright you are on road NL-230. On Gen 4 it's probably the NL-10 South of St. John's, but there might be more around.

lm.name: Exposed rock
lm.note: Just like in Ontario, it is common to find exposed rock lining the road in Newfoundland.

lm.name: Southwestern mountains
lm.note: The Southwestern edge of Newfoundland has a very distinct looking green mountain range visible from the Trans-Canada Highway.

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Bollards
lm.note:
Regular bollards are not too common in Newfoundland and Labrador, but you can sometimes find a rustic-looking wooden bollard at the end of the guardrails, as well as various interesting snowpoles.

Note: It is relatively common to see snowpoles on the side of residential driveways in NL.

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Double crossbar poletop
lm.note:
One of Newfoundland & Labrador's most common poletops is a trident poletop with double crossbars and thick insulators.

Note: The shape of the insulators can vary.

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Extra short lamp
lm.note:
Lamps with extra short arms are a unique feature of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Note: The rest of their lamps are similar to the old, curved lamps of Nova Scotia.

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Long trident poletop
lm.note:
The second most common poletop in Newfoundland and Labrador is a trident poletop with a low crossbar and long insulators.

Note: Manitoba's trident poletop looks similar, but that one has skinnier insulators and a second crossbar below the main one. (Not to mention the landscape couldn't be more different.)

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Metal plate
lm.note: A simple horizontal metal plate is hiding in plain sight on the utility poles of Newfoundland and Labrador.

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Provincial routes
lm.note:
Regular provincial routes in Newfoundland and Labrador are signed as a black number inside a white rectangle. They are organised regionally.

Useful to know:

  • 2 digit routes starting with a 2 are on the Avalon Peninsula
  • the 500s are in Labrador

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Short trident poletop
lm.note: The iconic long trident poletop of Newfoundland and Labrador has a very common variant with shorter vertical bars. The isulators can vary (usually stubby with 3 ribs or long with many ribs).

lm.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Wooden signpost
lm.note:
Within Atlantic Canada only Newfoundland and Labrador uses thick wooden signposts consistently.

Note: Nova Scotia has a mix of wooden and metal posts, while the rest of the Maritimes mostly uses square metal posts with small holes.

lm.name: Northwest Territories  - Canadian Shield
lm.note:
If you see exposed rocks by the road in the far Northwest, you are just North of the Great Slave Lake around Yellowknife (Roads NT-3 and 4).

Note: This is the Westernmost edge of the Canadian Shield.

lm.name: Northwest Territories  - Other bollards
lm.note:
The Northwest Territories has a few bollards not discussed on the Plonkit guide, even though many of them are more common than the Alberta-style variant. The two main types:

  • a hollow metal stick with a white or yellow rectangular part bolted on top
  • a square-shaped wooden bollard painted white

The exact designs are often specific to a certain road. (More about that on the Rural Roads map.)

lm.name: Northwest Territories  - Southern vibes
lm.note:
Southern Northwest Territories has a distinct vibe to it, featuring similar tall and skinny looking pines to Yukon but on a way flatter landscape.

Note: The whole Southern coverage is extremely sunny, except for some roads North and South of the Great Slave Lake.

lm.name: Northwest Territories  - Unpaved roads
lm.note:
The are only 3 unpaved roads in the Northwest Territories with official coverage:

  • the Dempster Highway (NT-8) to Inuvik
  • the Liard Highway (NT-7)
  • the MacKenzie Highway (NT-1) from a little South of Fort Simpson to a little West of the intersection with the NT-3

lm.name: Northwest Territories  - White highway post
lm.note: Just like Yukon, the Northwest Territories also use thick white wooden highway signposts.

lm.name: Bilingualism
lm.note: A little more than 10% of the inhabitants of Nova Scotia are bilingual. The most prominent Francophone areas are found on the Southern coast (centered around Yarmouth), the West coast of Cape Breton Island (Chéticamp, Margaree Harbour) and Southern Cape Breton Island (Isle Madame and surroundings). In these areas bilingual signs and the colours of the Acadian flag are a common sight.

lm.name: Green signback
lm.note: Green signbacks aren't exclusive to British Columbia and PEI: they are fairly common in Nova Scotia too. Here you will often find them supported by thick wooden or metal cross beams.

lm.name: Guardrail sticks
lm.note: Nova Scotia likes to place colourful snowpoles at the end of her guardrails. The most common style is yellow with a red reflector, but there are lots of possible variations.

lm.name: Hilly landscape
lm.note: Nova Scotia is generally hilly and has the thick vegetation typical of Eastern Canada. The highest elevation areas can be found on the Cape Breton Island, followed by the Cobequid Mountains on the mainland part.

lm.name: Isolated exit number
lm.note:
While highway signage in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick looks quite similar, only NS uses isolated exit numbers above the sign.

Note: The shape of the extra piece is useful, even when you view it from behind!

lm.name: Pokey guardrail
lm.note:
In Nova Scotia the wooden block that connects to the metal part of the guardrail is usually long enough to poke out under the guardrail. This is not the case in New Brunswick.

Note: The yellow reflectors are also more typical for Nova Scotia than for NB.

lm.name: Québec style poletop
lm.note:
It is fairly common to see Québec-style poletops in Nova Scotia, especially in the larger towns.

Note: The shape of the lamp attached will be different in the two provinces.

lm.name: Reflector guardrail
lm.note: Another common guardrail type in Nova Scotia is one without the extra woodblock. The yellow reflector tapes are still present on each leg.

lm.name: Short crossbeam poletop
lm.note:
The main poletop in Nova Scotia has a noticeably short and low crossbeam.

Note: The middle insulator is perpendicular to the wires.

lm.name: Short curved lamp
lm.note:
Lamps in Nova Scotia tend to have short, curved arms. There are 3 types of common lamp heads:

  • bulky and round (more on older coverage)
  • the "classic" square shaped
  • long and flat (more on newer coverage)

lm.name: Wire sticker
lm.note:
In Nova Scotia it is common to see red stickers wrapped around, or hanging from wires. The stickers can sometimes also show up in New Brunswick.

Note: The wire flags of Ontario and Québec can look very similar, but there you are more likely to see multiple stickers next to one another. Also, Nova Scotia doesn't use circle stickers. Look for other clues first!

lm.name: 3 tall ribbed insulators
lm.note:
Tall ribbed insulators are most common Ontario, followed by BC and NL. Crossarm poles with 3 tall ribbed insulators however are only found in Ontario.

Note: The 3 insulators can be upright or tilted.

lm.name: Bilingualism
lm.note:
English-French bilingualism within Ontario is typically found in the East. Main areas include Greater Sudbury, the Ottawa area close to the Québec border and around Kapuskasing in the Northeast.

Note: The region East of Sudbury has an excessive amount of bilingual signage.

lm.name: Blue cap guardrail
lm.note:
In some areas of Ontario, the standard wire guardrails have been replaced with a wire guardrail on steel posts with a blue cap on top.

Note: Highway 144 is a notable example, but it appears on many Northern highways on Gen 4.

lm.name: Colourful markings
lm.note: In Ontario it is common to see one or more colourful circles on the utility poles. Usually, they are red, blue or white, but I have also seen black and brown ones.

lm.name: County road sign
lm.note:
Southern Ontario uses a specific street sign design that includes the county name under the road name. They can also show numbers and direction arrows.

Note: These signs are most common in the extreme Southwest, but can also be found further East.

lm.name: Gen 3 snow
lm.note:
While most of the sunny Gen 3 snow coverage in Northwestern Ontario has been overwritten, there are still a few roads left where you can see it.

Full snow coverage:

  • between Eagle River and Sioux Lookout
  • ON 594 West of Dryden

Patchy, melting snow:

  • ON 622 around the Turtle River Provincial Park
  • ON 502 and ON 594 very close to Dryden

lm.name: Green electrical box
lm.note: This specific design of the green electrical box with the yellow numbers is common in residential areas throughout Ontario. Many of them also have a danger sticker or a circle sticker on it, although the numbers are enough to identify the design.

lm.name: GTA octo lamp
lm.note:
In the Greater Toronto Area a unique lamp can be found in large quantities. Although its top is usually very distinct, what makes it count as a meta is its octagonal shape and spotted grey colour.

Note: The post exists with more generic lamp heads too.

lm.name: Intersection pole ring
lm.note: In rural intersections in Southern Ontario you can sometimes encouter these short wooden poles with a ring on them. The ring can be white, yellow, orange or red and can appear on other signposts too. There are a few exception locations in Québec.

lm.name: Knotty fence
lm.note:
Wooden fences in Ontario are usually quite knotty and uneven. Prairie fences are smoother with a flat top.

Note: These fences are typically found in agricultural areas (St. Lawrence Lowlands and the Clay Belt).

lm.name: Larger top lamp
lm.note:
Ontario's traffic lights are unique, because the top lamp is larger than the bottom two. This is only true for 3-lamp setups, 4-lamp traffic lights are usually uniform.

Note: Rarely, you can find traffic lights without this feature in Ontario, especially in downtown Toronto.

lm.name: LCBO Stores
lm.note: The LCBO (Liquor Control Board of Ontario) is a chain of government-owned liquor stores that only operates in Ontario. Around the big Southern cities you can find large LCBO stores with spacious parking lots, while in the rural Northern towns small convenience store locations are more common.

lm.name: Longer crossarm
lm.note:
With a bit of training you might notice that Ontario uses a longer crossarm on its generic Canadian poles that most other provinces. In addition, the middle insulator will be parallel to the wire.

Note: Long crossarms can also be seen in Saskatchewan.

lm.name: Metal guardrail
lm.note: Besides wire guardrails, Ontario also uses metal guardrails with metal or wooden supports. Metal supports are common on large freeways, while the wooden ones are found on smaller highways.

lm.name: Northern red hydrants
lm.note:
Although most of Ontario uses yellow body fire hydrants, a few regional exceptions exist where the dominant hydrant colour is red.

Notable areas in Central and Northern Ontario:

  • Sault Ste Marie
  • a few towns around Lac Seul (Sioux Lookout, Dryden)
  • Nipigon
  • Fort Frances
  • a few smaller towns in the Clay Belt (Englehart, Earlton)

...and some other very tiny exceptions.

Note: Fire hydrants in the North tend to have a snow pole attached.

lm.name: Number stickers
lm.note:
Utility poles in Ontario can have a variety of yellow number stickers on them. Variants include a vertical sticker with 5-6 numbers, a horizontal version, and a much larger type with inverted colours.

Note: Some of the smaller yellow plates are fixed to the pole using 2 black rings.

lm.name: Paired boxes
lm.note: A green electrical box paired up with a small brown one is a common sight in the suburbs of far Southern Ontario.

lm.name: Railway poletop
lm.note: Nearby railway tracks in Ontario poles with a large number of small insulators can be present. These poletops can have a lot of extra crossarms.

lm.name: Rectangular signpost
lm.note:
The most common signpost in (semi) urban Ontario is a rectangular metal pole with small holes on it. Other provinces use solid or round signposts more often.

Note: In rural areas thick wooden signposts are even more common.

lm.name: Rural address colours
lm.note:
About 80% of rural adress signs in Ontario are green. Exceptions exist in the far West and far East of the province, where they are often blue.

Note: Within Canada, green rural address signs are more common West of Ontario and blue ones are more common East of it.

lm.name: Rural street sign
lm.note:
Rural street signs in Ontario are usually green, with white block letters in a specific font / style. The roads are often named "concession", "line" or "sideroad", especially on the far Southern grid.

Note: Many large cities (Toronto, Ottawa, Kitchener, Niagara Falls) use blue street signs instead.

lm.name: Silver numbers
lm.note:
Large silver numbers bolted on the utility poles are common in Ontario. They can be arranged vertically, diagonally or horizontally and usually you can also see the bolts holding them up.

Note: In reality, you will often find a mix of different markings on the pole.

lm.name: Small pole plate
lm.note: A very small, vertical pole plate made of metal can be found on utility poles accross Ontario.

lm.name: Southern architecture
lm.note:
Suburbs in Southern Ontario have a very distinct architectural style.

A few common features to look for:

  • the main building material is red brick
  • square roof vents or chimney shaped vents
  • trapezoid accent bricks
  • oval shaped gable windows
  • driveways being cut by sidewalks.

lm.name: Southern red hydrants
lm.note:
While most fire hydrants in Ontario are yellow, a few regional exceptions exist. In the South, the regions of Hamilton, Halton, Peel and some towns in Niagara consistently use red body hydrants.

Note: For some reason Grimsby, Lincoln and St. Catharines stick with yellow.

lm.name: Tilted attachment
lm.note:
A tilted attachment piece under the insulator is unique for Ontario. It can appear both on single insulator poles and the classic V-shape Ontario poletops, under the middle insulator. The insulators themselves are usually ribbed and sit parallel to the wire.

Note: V-poletops in BC don't have this attachment.

lm.name: V-shaped sewer cover
lm.note: The most prevalent sewer cover type in Ontario has a V-shape design. This is almost completely unique to Ontario.

lm.name: Wooden signpost
lm.note: In rural areas, Ontario likes to use thick, unpainted wooden signposts for information signs and traffic signs. Québec prefers metal.

lm.name: Yellow fire hydrants
lm.note:
Most of Ontario uses yellow-body fire hydrants. The nozzle and top colours vary from town to town and can be used for more specific guesses. (For more hydrant tips see: "Comprehensive Canada - Cities").

Note: There are a few notable sub-regions in Ontario with red fire hydrants.

lm.name: Ontario / British Columbia  - Secondary crossarm
lm.note:
Secondary crossarms on utility poles are typical in Ontario and British Columbia. To differentiate between the two provinces, you can check the following:

  • Ontario usually has a tilted attachment under the middle insulator
  • Ontario commonly uses a V-shape poletop or 3 ribbed insulators, while BC prefers white mushrooms
  • secondary crossarms in BC are usually longer.

Note: In the Prairies you will only see large secondary crossarm poles with downward facing insulators. The Maritimes don't use secondary crossarms.

lm.name: Ontario / British Columbia  - Tilted insulators
lm.note:
Poletops with 3 tilted insulators are commonly found in British Columbia and Ontario.

Tips to differentiate:

  • tall, ribbed insulators are always Ontario
  • BC prefers "mushrooms" or UFO-shaped insulators
  • tilted insulators in a 2+1 pattern are BC only.

Note: I have seen tilted insulator poletops in Nova Scotia too. Look at the colour of the wood to rule it out!

lm.name: Ontario / Manitoba  - Mini insulators
lm.note:
Insulators that are visibly smaller than the standard can be found in Ontario and Manitoba. They can appear on single insulator poles or full crossarm poletops.

Note: Mini insulators can sometimes appear in Saskatchewan and rarely in Alberta too.

lm.name: Ontario / Québec  - Corn production
lm.note:
Most of Canada's corn production happens in Southern Ontario and Québec, in the St. Lawrence Lowlands.

Note: Wheat and canola are more common in the Clay Belt and the Prairies.

lm.name: Ontario / Québec  - Curve ahead signs
lm.note:
You can tell Ontario and Québec apart by their curve ahead signs: the ones in Ontario curve noticeably less than the ones in Québec.

Note: The post material will also be different.

lm.name: Ontario / Québec  - Farms
lm.note:
The farms on the St. Lawrence Lowlands have a very unique architectural style. The most distinct are the white top circular grain silos and the roof shape of the stables.

The following elements are more typical for Ontario (and extreme SW Québec) than Québec:

  • fancy vents and roof decorations
  • multiple large grain silos
  • horses

lm.name: Ontario / Québec  - Wire flags
lm.note: Orange flags and circles are quite common to find on wires near the pole in Ontario and Québec. The circles can be yellow too.

lm.name: Prairies  - Orange-red wire marker
lm.note:
Orange-red underground wire markers can be found in all three Prairie Provinces. They are the most consistent in Alberta.

Note: In Saskatchewan, yellow markers are also common.

lm.name: Prairies  - Smooth fence
lm.note: Wooden fences on the Prairies tend to be smooth, with a flat top. (Fences in Ontario usually have knots and are of worse quality).

lm.name: Bilingual street sign
lm.note: Bilingualism on Prince Edward Island is regional: it is more present in the West, especially in the Evangeline region (West of Summerside). Despite this, most street signs will be bilingual in the province, while the STOP signs will be in English only.

lm.name: Hilly areas
lm.note:
While most of Prince Edward Island is quite flat, you can find rolling hills in a few notable areas:

  1. West of Charlottetown
  2. Just South of Montague
  3. In the Far Northeast, North of Souris

lm.name: Ribbed insulator poletops
lm.note: A distinct poletop with 3 long thin ribbed insulators can be found on Prince Edward Island. A variant of this poletop with 2 angled up brackets, just like an Ontario poletop is specific to the region North of Montague.

lm.name: Standard pole
lm.note:
The most dominant pole on Prince Edward Island is similar to the Nova Scotia pole (insulators perpendicular to the wire, crossbar not as high up as in NB), but it has a slightly longer crossbar.

Note: The lamps can be both NB and NS style.

lm.name: Appalachian vibes
lm.note:
South of the St. Lawrence River in Québec a rolling landscape can be seen with a mix of pines (mostly Eastern White pine) and broadleaf trees. This area is part of the Appalachian Mountains so it can look a lot like the neighbouring states of the US (Maine, Vermont or New Hampshire).

Note: The elevation gets much higher as you get to the Gaspé peninsula in the East.

lm.name: Cement block
lm.note: In Québec, wires leading to the ground often feed into a covered cement block at the base of the pole.

lm.name: Curved lamp
lm.note:
Lamps in Québec curve more than in other provinces.

Note: They are longer than the curved lamps found in the Maritimes.

lm.name: Double signpost
lm.note: In Québec signs are often held up by 2 metal signposts.

lm.name: Gaspé lamp
lm.note: S-curve lamps are typically found on the Gaspé Peninsula. Many of them have an extra support bar below.

lm.name: Guardrail endings
lm.note:
In Québec, guardrails can end in 2 ways:

  • flat, with black and yellow stripes
  • in a simple hoop.

In both cases you will see a snow pole-like bollard at the end of the guardrail.

lm.name: Horizontal stoplight
lm.note: Québec uses horizontal stoplights. Most of them are fully black, but yellow outlines are also common.

lm.name: Laurentides
lm.note:
North of the St. Lawrence River you can see the Laurentian Mountain Range. The densely forested mountains get taller the further East you go with some impressive heights just North of Québec City.

Note: The Laurentides are part of the Canadian Shield, so exposed rocks lining the road in a green montainous environment is a good clue for the area. You won't get mountains of this size in Ontario.

lm.name: Metal signpost
lm.note:
In comparison to other provinces, Québec uses a lot of metal signposts. They usually have little holes on them.

Note: This comes in handy for Ontario - Québec 50/50s as Ontario prefers thick wooden posts in rural areas.

lm.name: Snowmobile sign
lm.note: Designated snowmobile trails are common in Québec, especially on the Northern roads. They are indicated by yellow diamond signs with the pictogram of a snowmobile, or more rarely also a quad bike.

lm.name: Southwestern cross
lm.note: Cross signbacks are a good clue for Southwestern Québec. (Usually on the plains South of Montréal).

lm.name: Unique lamp arm
lm.note: Double lamp arms with 2 vertical bars in between are unique to Québec.

lm.name: Québec / New Brunswick  - T pole
lm.note:
On generic poletops, the horizontal crossbar is higher up in Québec and New Brunswick than in the other Canadian provinces. (The pole looks more like a "T" than a "t".)

Note: Middle insulators in Québec are perpendicular to the wire, in NB they are parallel.

lm.name: Québec / Nova Scotia  - Perpendicular insulator
lm.note:
In Québec, Nova Scotia and on Prince Edward Island middle insulators (or standalone insulators) will be perpendicular to the wire.

Note: Parallel is the Canadian standard.

lm.name: "Alberta" bollards
lm.note:
Bollards are a rare sight in Sask due to the straighness of their roads, but beware: on major roads you can sometimes see "Alberta-style" bollards. Manitoba-style ones are also possible, but these are even rarer.

Note: Most of Sask's bollards are found in highway intersections close to one of the largest cities. If you see a bollard on a random rural road you are probably somewhere else.

lm.name: Blank metal strip
lm.note:
Rural pole stickers in Saskatchewan can be quite random, but a completely blank silver metal strip is commonly seen.

Note: Alberta has a similar sticker, but it is more likely to feature numbers. Use with caution.

lm.name: Extreme flatness
lm.note:
Saskatchewan is a very flat province - even by Prairies standards.

Note: Do no forget about the barren Cypress Hills of the Far Southwest!

lm.name: Gas pipeline marker
lm.note:
Upon leaving rural towns in Sask it is very common to see high pressure natural gas pipelines marked by a warning sign unique to the province. The sign can be white or red, with an oval shape on top saying "DANGER".

Note: It can be found in rolled up form too, like the underground wire markers.

lm.name: Green lamp
lm.note:
Isolated lamps in Saskatchewan are often green.

Note: They are commonly seen in suburbs and small towns.

lm.name: Guardrail loop
lm.note: Guardrails are quite rare in Saskatchewan, but when you do see them they end in an open loop and lack the holes seen on Alberta guardrails.

lm.name: Lamp support
lm.note: Lamps in Saskatchewan are often curved and have a support bar underneath. (About 60% of their lamps are like this.)

lm.name: Long crossarm pole
lm.note:
If you can't find typical 2+1 alternating insulator poletops in Sask, you can still rely on the excessive lenght of the crossbar to identify the province.

Note: Ontario also likes long crossarms.

lm.name: Lower insulator
lm.note: In Saskatchewan, you can sometimes find insulators that are mounted lower than the generic Canadian ones. Not every insulator will be like this, but it is a unique feature of Sask.

lm.name: Northern vegetation
lm.note: The further North you go in Saskatchewan, the more vegetation you will see. The absolute flatness of the Prairies gradually gives way to boreal forests on slightly hillier terrain.

lm.name: Rare poletops
lm.note:
Northern Saskatchewan is home to a wide range of intriguing poletops.

Note: The "missing insulator pole" in Alberta is missing its insulator on the bottom bar, otherwise it is similar to the one in the example.

lm.name: Rural road quality
lm.note: Rural roads in Saskatchewan tend to be thinner and in a worse condition than in Alberta (or Manitoba). Roads that have been patched up a few times are a common sight here.

lm.name: Rural street sign
lm.note:
Rural street signs in Saskatchewan are usually green with white letters. Be careful: calling roads "range road" or "township road" aren't exclusive to Alberta - they are also common here!

Note: Most of Alberta's rural street signs are blue.

lm.name: White signpost
lm.note:
White-painted wooden signposts are commonly found in Saskatchewan.

Note: Yukon and NWT often use white wooden signposts for their highway signs, but not for their small traffic signs.

lm.name: Yellow wire marker
lm.note:
While orange/red underground wire markers are the standard within the Prairies, Saskatchewan also uses yellow markers. These are unique within the Prairies.

Note: Yellow markers are also typical in Ontario, Québec and BC.

lm.name: Saskatchewan / Manitoba  - Weird guardrails
lm.note:
While guardrails in general are quite rare in the Prairies, you can sometimes come accross a few alternative guardrails in Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

  • in Sask, this means either a wire guardrail with 2 wires close together or a short square wooden guardrail
  • in Manny, it's usually a wire guardrail with 3 wires

Note: Alberta prefers "normal" guardrails.

lm.name: Complicated crossbeam
lm.note: Utility poles in Yukon can have rather complicated secondary crossbeams. They can be assymmetrical or twisted and they usually have a number of extra insulators on them.

lm.name: Orange tint pole
lm.note: Most utility poles in Yukon are generic T-poles with a distinct orange tint.

lm.name: Pink fireweed
lm.note:
Fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium) is Yukon's floral emblem. While it can be found all over the province, you can only see the bright pink flowers bloom on the Gen 2 July coverage. This means 2 main areas in the far South:

  • on Route 3 (Haines Road) between the Dezadeash Lake and the BC border
  • the roads Southeast of Whitehorse (the area around Tagish)
  • on Route 1 (Alaska Highway) around Upper Liard and also West of it

Note: On Gen 4 you will see the leaves and stems of the plant changing into dark reddish Autumn colours. Autumn fireweed has a larger range.

lm.name: September 2022
lm.note:
The newer Gen 4 coverage in Yukon was captured in September (©2022). It is easy to recognise from the extremely vibrant yellow-orange Autumn colours.

Note: Yukon has only Gen 2 and Gen 4.

lm.name: Snowpoles
lm.note:
Instead of bollards, Yukon prefers to use a variety of thin snowpoles. Most common designs: thick stripes of 2 colours, or one base colour + a different top. The snowpoles come in handy in border 50/50-s with BC or NWT which use their own bollards.

Note: The exact pattern of colours is often specific to a certain road. (More on that in the Rural Roads map.)

lm.name: Treeless mountains
lm.note: Mountains in Yukon are mostly treeless and brownish of colour. They are usually seen in the distance.

lm.name: Unpaved roads
lm.note:
Knowing which roads are unpaved is useful in Yukon. The largest cluster is in the East, on the Route 4 (Robert Campbell Highway) between Faro and Tuchitua and its offroads including Route 6.

Secondly, Routes 5 (Dempster Higway) and 9 (Top of the World Highway) in the far North are unpaved too.

lm.name: White highway post
lm.note:
Highway signposts in Yukon are usually made of thick white-painted wood.

Note: NWT also uses white signposts. BC prefers them unpainted.

lm.name: Yukon / British Columbia  - Cloudy border
lm.note:
Gen 2 coverage with very gloomy, cloudy weather can be found on both sides of the BC - Yukon border.

Note: The pictures were taken in July so you can sometimes see pink fireweed around. (©2019)

lm.name: BC Guardrail
lm.note: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.

lm.name: Newfoundland/Labrador Guardrail
lm.note: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.

lm.name: Ontario Guardrail
lm.note: In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.

lm.name: Saskatchewan white bits
lm.note: Yellow center lines in Saskatchewan frequently have tiny white bits in and around them. You can also rarely find them in BC and Yukon, but the landscape there should be different enough to not get them confused.

lm.name: Single Yellow
lm.note:
• Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines.
  • However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.

--- NOTE:

  • Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US.
  • This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.

lm.name: Checkboard sign
lm.note: This diamond-shaped T-intersection "checkboard" sign is unique to Canada.

lm.name: Maximum sign
lm.note: Canadian speed limit signs have the word "Maximum," while U.S. signs use "Speed Limit."

lm.name: Quebec stop sign.
lm.note: Stop signs with the word ‘Arret’ are unique to Quebec in Canada.

lm.name: Alberta bollard
lm.note: Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

lm.name: Ontario diamonds
lm.note: You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.

lm.name: Ontario speed signs
lm.note: Ontario speed limit signs may feature a black section at the bottom, with the words "km/h" or "begins" written in white.

lm.name: Manitoba stop signs
lm.note: You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.

lm.name: Newfoundland T-intersection sign
lm.note: Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.

lm.name: Ontario guard rails
lm.note: In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.

lm.name: Quebec double sign post
lm.note: Double sign posts on warning sings in Canada is unique to Quebec.

lm.name: Quebec guardrail bollards
lm.note: Quebec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

lm.name: Quebec pole stickers
lm.note: Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.

lm.name: Quebec rectangle markers
lm.note: You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary.

lm.name: Sask stop sign white triangles.
lm.note: Those white triangles(can be different ammount of them) on signposts of stop signs are unique to Saskatchewan.

lm.name: Sask white dashes between lines
lm.note: Those white dashes between yellow lines are most commonly found in Saskatchewan. You can also sometimes find them in BC but the landscape will be way different.

lm.name: Saskatchewan alternating insulators
lm.note:
Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.

NOTE: This can rarely be seen in Manitoba.
