lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines.
  • However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.

NOTE: Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US. This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.

lm.name: 2 side 1 top
lm.note:
These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.

lm.name: Quebec pole
lm.note: Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.

lm.name: Québec polelabel
lm.note: Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.

lm.name: Saska pole
lm.note: Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.

lm.name: small white sticker
lm.note: Poles on Prince Edward Island usually feature a small white sticker.

lm.name: Transfo 45° angle
lm.note: Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.

lm.name: Transfo faced road
lm.note: The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.

lm.name: Abbotsford  - White hydrant
lm.note: Abbotsford, British Columbia can be recognised by its white fire hydrants with a blue top and nozzles.

lm.name: Amherst  - Yellow body hydrant
lm.note:
While most cities in Nova Scotia use red body fire hydrants, there are some notable yellow exceptions. Amherst uses a yellow hydrant with a black nozzle and occasionally a black top.

Note: The town also has some fully yellow variants.

lm.name: Barrie  - Downtown street sign
lm.note: Barrie is the most significant city in Simcoe county. The downtown area has some unique black street signs indicating the neighbourhood in a "Historic XY" format.

lm.name: Barrie  - Street sign lines
lm.note:
Barrie is the most significant city in Simcoe county. Outside of a few downtown neighbourhoods Barrie uses a green street sign with a metal line on the top and the bottom.

Note: The downtown area has its own unique street sign which is black.

lm.name: Brandon  - Blue bus stops
lm.note:
Brandon Manitoba has 2 kinds of bus stops:

  • a light blue rectangular sign commonly seen on Gen 3 coverage
  • a dark blue shark fin shape sign only seen on Gen 4 / main roads.

lm.name: Brandon  - Rusted yellow hydrant
lm.note:
Brandon Manitoba uses these rusted yellow fire hydrants.

Note: Top and nozzle colours can vary.

lm.name: Brandon  - Street sign clasps
lm.note: Brandon uses a green street sign with metal clasps which are different to Winnipeg's.

lm.name: Brooklin  - Fancy roof ridge
lm.note: These designs on the end of roof ridges and dormers are extremely common in the town of Brooklin.

lm.name: Burnaby  - "Clown" hydrant
lm.note: Burnaby, a satellite city just East of Vancouver uses a distinct colour scheme for its fire hydrants: a white body, red nozzles and a green top. Just like a clown's makeup!

lm.name: Calgary  - Big trees
lm.note:
Calgary has a lot of big trees right up against people's homes.

Note: Obviously, Calgary won't be the only Canadian city where this happens.

lm.name: Calgary  - Calgary Transit
lm.note: Calgary uses dark blue bus stops and red buses.

lm.name: Calgary  - Neon hydrant
lm.note: Calgary fire hydrants are neon green with black nozzles. Very easy to spot!

lm.name: Calgary  - No cap signpost
lm.note: Calgary's signposts have small casps and no cap. Edmonton's have small holes and a cap instead.

lm.name: Calgary  - Yellow traffic light
lm.note: Calgary's traffic lights are fully yellow on both sides. Edmonton's are fully black on the front and Red Deer's are black in the middle with a yellow frame.

lm.name: Cambridge Bay  - Landmark trekkers
lm.note:
Just accross the river from Cambridge Bay there are some interesting trekkers showing 3 landmarks. From North to South, these are:

  • A distinctly shaped monument to Roald Amundsen's polar ship "The Maud" with the actual shipwreck still in the bay
  • The Old Stone Church
  • Ruins of the Old Town.

lm.name: Cambridge Bay  - Surrounding roads
lm.note:
Cambridge Bay has coverage on 2 roads surrounding the town:

  • the road to the Airport (West) has poles on the South/West side and snow poles on the other,
  • the road to the Cemetery (East) has water to the South/East.

lm.name: Cambridge Bay  - Vibes
lm.note: Cambridge Bay coverage is wet, rainy and overcast. It is the only Gen 2 coverage in Nunavut, leaving this large pink blur in the sky - similar to Inuvik.

lm.name: Carcross  - Vibes
lm.note: Carcross is surrounded by large mountains and water in all directions: Nares Lake to the East and Bennett Lake to the West. All coverage is cloudy Gen 2.

lm.name: Carmacks  - Wooden street sign
lm.note: Carmacks has wooden street signs, just like Haines Junction. To identify Carmacks, look for the plain rectangular shape, the letters in italics and the brown signposts.

lm.name: Carmacks  - Yellow lamp
lm.note:
You can identify the Klondike Highway going through Carmacks by the rusty yellow lamps.

Note: In true Yukon fashion, the lamps often have flags on them.

lm.name: Carmacks  - Yukon River & hills
lm.note: Carmacks is located on the Yukon River and is surrounded by hills. While the town and the banks of the river has Gen 2 coverage only, the Klondike Highway and the Carmacks Bridge has Gen 4.

lm.name: Charlottetown  - Asymmetrical poletop
lm.note:
Charlottetown uses a lot of asymmetrical poletops. They can have single or multiple insulator rods.

Note: Charlottetown also has some poletops that look similar to the ones used in Québec.

lm.name: Charlottetown  - Horizontal traffic light
lm.note:
Prince Edward Island uses horizontal black traffic lights, just like Québec. This is only really applicable to Charlottetown.

Note: These diamond and square shaped lamps seem to be unique to PEI.

lm.name: Charlottetown  - Red hydrant with green nozzles
lm.note:
Charlottetown uses red fire hydrants with a green top and green nozzles.

Note: On Gen 3 the nozzles are more generic grey.

lm.name: Chilliwack  - Green-on-white street sign
lm.note: Chilliwack uses these unique green-on-white street signs. Also notice the metal sign clasps typical for South-Western B.C.

lm.name: Churchill  - Antenna
lm.note:
The overcast Gen3 snow coverage in Churchill Manitoba can look similar to the Nunavut trekkers. Use the antenna on the right side on the car to recognise the town!

Note: The town has unique street signs.

lm.name: Churchill Falls  - Halloween
lm.note:
Churchill Falls was covered around Halloween, so it is common to see Halloween decorations on people's homes.

Note: Churchill Falls is a scary town.

lm.name: Churchill Falls  - Hills to the East
lm.note:
Churchill Falls can be recognised by its sunny Gen 4 coverage and two distinctive hills to the East.

Note: One is shaped like a lopsided pyramid, the other one has two bumps on top.

lm.name: Churchill Falls  - Red hydrant with grey nozzle
lm.note: Churchill Falls has red body fire hydrants with a grey nozzle. It is commonly accompanied by a Québec-style hydrant marker of a yellow or red colour.

lm.name: Churchill Falls  - Unique lamp
lm.note: This stylish lamp with a yellow sticker, standing on a concrete block is extremely common in Churchill Falls.

lm.name: Corner Brook  - Hilliness
lm.note: Corner Brook is situated on a large hill and can be identified most of the time because of its hilliness.

lm.name: Corner Brook  - Hydrant numbers
lm.note: Corner Brook marks all fire hydrants with numbers.

lm.name: Dauphin  - Black signpost
lm.note: Dauphin is a smaller town in Manitoba that follows all the same meta as Winnipeg: red fire hydrants, white street signs. The main difference is that Dauphin uses black sign posts for its street signs.

lm.name: Dawson City  - Airport Road
lm.note: This unique pole type runs from Dawson City to the Airport on the South side of the road. This combined with the foggy weather makes the road extremely easy to recognise.

lm.name: Dawson City  - Foggy mountains
lm.note: Dawson City is built in a valley. You will feel surrounded by epic mountains. A lot of the coverage is foggy, making the mountains barely visible.

lm.name: Dawson City  - Frontier-style architecture
lm.note: Dawson City's colourful frontier-style architecture makes the town look like a set for a Western movie.

lm.name: Dawson City  - July 2009
lm.note: The highlighted roads around Dawson City feature some unique July 2009 coverage. This coverage appears to be extremely dry and has a warm tinge to it. The birch trees will have a very bright white colour, similar to what is seen in Manitoba.

lm.name: Dawson City  - Unique street sign
lm.note: Dawson City uses uniquely shaped white street signs. Signposts are typically black or very rusted.

lm.name: Dawson Creek  - "Smokey" with thin aspens
lm.note: The Dawson Creek region resembles Alberta with its flatness and its abundance of thin aspen trees. Older generation Dawson Creek coverage has a distinct "smokey feel" to it.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Alleyway coverage
lm.note:
Edmonton has a lot of alleyway coverage.

Note: This type of coverage can be found in other large Canadian cities as well. Luckily, garbage bins with the city's logo and name are abundant in alleys.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Black traffic lights
lm.note:
Edmonton's traffic lights are fully black on the front and yellow on the back.

Note: Calgary's are yellow on both sides and Red Deer's are black in the middle with a yellow frame.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Blue nozzle hydrant
lm.note: Edmonton fire hydrants have a yellow body with a blue top and nozzles.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Edmonton Transit System
lm.note:
Edmonton uses blue buses, blue bus stops and blue shelters.

Note: Sometimes you can see the ETS logo on them (Edmonton Transit System).

lm.name: Edmonton  - Holey signpost
lm.note: Edmonton's signposts have small holes on the back and often have a cap on top. Calgary's have small casps and no cap.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Lamp sticker
lm.note: If you see a red sticker on the base of a lamp, it's 100% Edmonton. About half of the lamps have red, but you can also find it in white.

lm.name: Edmonton  - Large base lamp
lm.note: In Edmonton many lamps have a large metal box for a base.

lm.name: Edmundston  - Yellow hydrant with grey nozzle
lm.note:
Edmundston is the only major city in New Brunswick to use yellow fire hydrants. The nozzles are grey.

Note: Edmunston also uses Québec-style hydrant markers in various colours.

lm.name: Enterprise  - Asymmetrical road lanes and bollards
lm.note: The best way to identify Enterprise is by the asymmetrical (2/1) road lanes. Apart from that, there are various bollards.

lm.name: Estevan  - Yellow infrastructure
lm.note:
Estevan really likes the colour yellow. Yellow signposts, yellow fire hydrans, yellow curbs.

Note: Sadly, their lamps are green.

lm.name: Faro  - Vibes
lm.note: Faro has limited and choppy Gen 4 coverage. It has a bright sunset with clear skies and a medium sized hill visible to the North. Faro also has some unique street signs indicating the town's name.

lm.name: Flin Flon  - Brown street sign
lm.note: Flin Flon uses unique brown street signs. This is a very consistent clue.

lm.name: Flin Flon  - Red-black hydrant
lm.note:
Flin Flon uses red fire hydrants with a black top and lots of yellow curbs.

Note: While none of these features are unique to Flin Flon, these together with the hazy Gen4 coverage is enough to identify the city.

lm.name: Flin Flon  - The Stack
lm.note: Flin Flon's iconic blue-grey chimney, "The Stack" is visible from far away. (Especially from the Western part of the city.)

lm.name: Fort Frances  - Dark red hydrant
lm.note: Fort Frances features a dark red hydrant with a matching snow pole.

lm.name: Fort Frances  - Maple leaf street sign
lm.note: This fun looking maple leaf logo street sign is unique to Fort Frances. Note: They are only found downtown.

lm.name: Fort Liard  - Vibes
lm.note:
Fort Liard has only one road of coverage in town: Valley Main Street. It can be identified by:

  • the Québec-style curved lamps with a slight upward tilt and Québec-style connection pieces,
  • the yellow pole stickers,
  • the generic green street signs.

lm.name: Fort Mc Murray  - Blue street sign
lm.note: Fort Mc Murray is one of the only cities in Alberta that uses blue street signs. This is different from the rural ones which are almost always blue. Additionally, this street sign has no cardinal directions on it.

lm.name: Fort Mc Murray  - North white aspen trees
lm.note: Fort McMurray is easily identifiable from the north white aspen trees.

lm.name: Fort Mc Pherson  - Clear weather & long leg crates
lm.note:
Fort McPherson is a town located on the Dempster Highway. It looks a lot like Inuvik, but with clearer weather. Both towns have Gen 2 only.

Note: In Fort McPherson wooden garbage crates often have longer "legs" than in the other NWT towns.

lm.name: Fort Simpson  - Vibes
lm.note:
Fort Simpson has one road of coverage: 100 St. South of the town this road will have guardrails with a lot of NWT bollards on them. Inside the town you will see Québec-style curved lamps and connection pieces, similar to the ones in Fort Liard.

Note: Fort Simpson has wider roads and looks more residential than Fort Liard.

lm.name: Fredericton  - Blue street sign
lm.note: Fredericton uses exclusively blue street signs. Most of New Brunswick uses green.

lm.name: Fredericton  - Red hydrant with blue nozzle
lm.note: Fredericton uses red body fire hydrants with blue nozzles.

lm.name: Gander  - White street sign with black text
lm.note: Gander uses white street signs, sometimes with bold black text.

lm.name: Gander  - Yellow marker
lm.note: Gander uses a yellow pole to mark its fire hydrants instead of a diamond.

lm.name: Gatineau  - Oval logo
lm.note: Gatineau's distinct oval logo shows up on street signs and garbage bins throughout the whole city.

lm.name: Granby  - Logo streetsign
lm.note: Granby uses this unique logo on street signs.

lm.name: Granby  - STOP sign
lm.note: For some reason, the whole city of Granby uses "STOP" signs instead of the Québec "Arrêt". This might be the only place in Québec to do so.

lm.name: Granby  - Yellow border hydrant marker
lm.note: Granby often uses a unique blue hydrant marker with a yellow border.

lm.name: Grande Prairie  - Aquatera bin
lm.note: These grey garbage cans that say "Aquatera" are common and unique to Grande Prairie.

lm.name: Grande Prairie  - Period street sign
lm.note: Grande Prairie always puts a period at the end of their street names.

lm.name: Grande Prairie  - Yellow hydrant
lm.note: Grande Prairie is one of the only places in Alberta with yellow fire hydrants.

lm.name: Grise Fjord  - Vibes
lm.note: Grise Fjord should be instantly recognisable by the unique mountains which are visible from all locs. Looking down, most of the time you can see the corner of a red quad bike. The trekker along the beach doesn't have the quad bike but the sea ice and the mountains give it away.

lm.name: Haines Junction  - Mt. Martha Black
lm.note: The best way to identify Haines Junction is by the large mountain range to the Southwest called Mt. Martha Black. The town is also built on a hill: North is uphill, South is down. The range to the North is sometimes also visible, but much smaller.

lm.name: Haines Junction  - Red and yellow hydrants
lm.note: Haines Junction fire hydrants can be red with yellow nozzles or fully yellow.

lm.name: Haines Junction  - Street signs
lm.note:
Haines Junction's official street sign is made of wood. There are about 10 of these in the town, the rest of the signs are green with a white border, standard in Yukon.

Note: Carmacks also has wooden street signs, but they are more rectangular and never have green signposts.

lm.name: Halifax  - Fake Québec poletop
lm.note:
Halifax has a lot of these "Québec-like" poletops. Within Nova Scotia, this is mostly a Halifax thing.

Note: This poletop shows up in various places within Atlantic Canada, including NS. Only go Halifax if see a lot of it and you feel like you are in a big enough city.

lm.name: Halifax  - Flat lamp
lm.note: Lamps in Halifax have a distinct flat shape.

lm.name: Halifax  - Halifax Transit
lm.note: Halifax Transit has a distinct white-blue-yellow colour scheme that appears on buses and bus stops as well. Their designs often involve the letter "X" - or at least a part of it.

lm.name: Halifax  - Orange hydrant
lm.note: Halifax uses unique orange fire hydrants. Dartmouth, on the opposite side of the Bedford Basin uses the standard red hydrants of Nova Scotia.

lm.name: Halifax  - Tufts Cove smokestacks
lm.note: The smokestacks of the Tufts Cove Generating Station are an integral part of the Halifax skyline. The station is located in the neighbouring Dartmouth and has 3 tall chimneys with red and white stripes that can be spotted from far away.

lm.name: Hamilton  - Attached stop sign
lm.note: Stop signs in Hamilton are often attached perpendicular to a sign or post, this is rare in Ontario.

lm.name: Hamilton  - Blue Area strip
lm.note: Speed signs in Hamilton often have a blue "area" strip. This can be occasionally found elsewhere in Ontario, but are especially common in Hamilton.

lm.name: Happy Valley - Architecture
lm.note: Architecture in Happy Valley-Goose Bay is characterised by light coloured buildings with generally flat roofs.

lm.name: Happy Valley - Coverage
lm.note:
Happy Valley-Goose Bay can be identified by its:

  • gloomy November Gen 4 coverage
  • relative flatness with blue ridges in the distance
  • being larger than any other town in Labrador
  • extreme sandiness.

Note: North West River looks similar, but way hillier.

lm.name: Happy Valley - Hydrant variants
lm.note:
The classic Happy Valley-Goose Bay fire hydrant is red with a yellow top and blue nozzles. A more modest-looking red variant is also common there.

Note: The rainbow coloured ones usually come with a little red-white flag as a marker.

lm.name: Happy Valley - Short lamp
lm.note: Happy Valley-Goose Bay uses a very short style of lamp.

lm.name: Inner Vancouver  - Red hydrant
lm.note:
The City of Vancouver proper uses uniform red fire hydrants.

Note: Satellite cities such as Surrey, Burnaby, or North Vancouver use different colours.

lm.name: Inukjuak  - Vibes
lm.note:
Inukjuak is a town on the coast of the Hudson Bay in Northern Québec. It can be recognised by the snowmobile coverage with the distinct rearview mirrors and the blurred driver.

Sanikiuaq looks similar, but there you can see a driver wearing a brown coat.

lm.name: Inuvik  - Garbage crates
lm.note: In Inuvik, large wooden or metal garbage crates can be found at the end of many driveways. They are similar to what you see in Yellowknife.

lm.name: Inuvik  - Pink Gen 2 blur
lm.note: Inuvik shows up a lot on the default Canada map because of its northernliness. You can recognise it by its gloomy weather and the extremely pink Gen 2 blur on the sky.

lm.name: Inuvik  - Yellow guardrail & bollard
lm.note: The Northern town of Inuvik boasts some unique yellow guardrails and a yellow bollard.

lm.name: Iqaluit  - Fortified hydrant
lm.note:
Fire hydrants in Iqualuit are quite unique: they are "fortified" by 3-4 thick red bollards and a triangular marker.

Note: Sometimes the bollards don't have a hydrant in the middle.

lm.name: Iqaluit / Apex  - Bilingual signs
lm.note: In Iqualuit and Apex street signs, stop signs and pretty much everything else is bilingual in the Inuktitut and English languages.

lm.name: Iqaluit / Apex  - Road to Apex
lm.note: The road between Iqaluit and Apex can be identified by the bollards and the poles. It's also worth mentioning that Iqaluit is a trekker, so the camera is on the side of the road, not the middle.

lm.name: Kamloops  - 2 bolts street sign
lm.note:
Kamloops uses this unique green street sign with two bolts on the left side.

Note: Kelowna street signs are blue with no bolts.

lm.name: Kamloops  - White top hydrant
lm.note:
Fire hydrants in Kamloops are yellow with a white top and nozzles. This distinguishes them from Kelowna hydrants which use different top colours.

Tip: In general, cities between Prince George and the US border will have yellow hydrants, while Eastern and Western BC uses red.

lm.name: Kangiqsuallujuaq  - Vibes
lm.note:
Kangiqsuallujuaq is a town in far Northern Québec. It can be identified by the green rocky hills surrounding it, with trees visible in the distance.

Note: I think the hills give a vaguely North-European vibe.

lm.name: Kelowna  - Fruit plantations
lm.note: The Okanagan Valley is very distinct. It has a semi-arid climate and can look almost mediterranean. In and around Kelowna fruit plantations (orchards, vinyards) are a common sight.

lm.name: Kelowna  - Green bus stop
lm.note: Kelowna has a lot of green bus stops and a blue street sign with white letters. The street sign can have a few variations.

lm.name: Kelowna  - Yellow hydrant
lm.note:
While the classic Kelowna fire hydrant is yellow with a blue top, other colour variations exist in the city. The most common variant has an orange top and nozzles.

Tip: In general, cities between Prince George and the US border will have yellow hydrants, while Eastern and Western BC uses red.

lm.name: Kenora  - "Manitoba" dirt
lm.note: In Kenora the dirt has a similar light colour to what you would find in Manitoba. Note: This dirt is often visible on the pavement too.

lm.name: Kenora  - Exposed rocks
lm.note: Kenora is quite hilly and has exposed rocks even on residential streets.

lm.name: Kenora  - Yellow hydrant with red pole
lm.note: Kenora fire hydrants are yellow and always have a red snow pole attached.

lm.name: Kingston  - Black lamps
lm.note: Downtown Kingston (mainly Princess St. and Queen St.) has unique black traffic lights and lamps.

lm.name: Kingston  - White pole sticker
lm.note: In Kingston lamps and utility poles are tagged with a white sticker with numbers on it. This is a consistent meta.

lm.name: Kingston  - White sticker hydrant
lm.note: Kingston has a white sticker with the letter "H" followed by numbers on its fire hydrants. This is a very consistent meta.

lm.name: Kitchener  - Extra thicc sign border
lm.note: Twin cities Kitchener and Waterloo both use these extra thick white outline sign borders. Note: Kitchener mostly uses blue while Waterloo prefers green.

lm.name: Kitchener / Waterloo  - Arched bus stop
lm.note: Twin cities Kitchener and Waterloo feature bus stops with a uniquely arched shape.

lm.name: Labrador City  - Northwest hills and poletop
lm.note: Labrador City has only one road of coverage. This road can be recognised by the hills to the Northwest and the tall wooden poles with a trident poletop.

lm.name: Lake Ontario area  - Red body hydrant
lm.note:
The West Coast of Lake Ontario (the regions of Hamilton, Halton, Peel and Niagara Falls) most commonly uses red body hydrants. Generally, the rest of Ontario uses a yellow body.

Note: St. Catharines uses the usual Ontario yellows.

lm.name: Lethbridge  - Street sign layout
lm.note:
Lethbridge uses the street number - kind of street - cardinal direction format for its street signs.

Note: Calgary and Medicine hat uses block capital letters for the kind of street. Lethbridge only capitalizes the first letter.

lm.name: London  - Black number sticker
lm.note: This unique black sticker is found on almost every pole in London. They can start with a letter (mostly "SW", "T" or "P") or just feature 5 numbers without any letter.

lm.name: London  - LT Symbol
lm.note: The London Transit Commission has a recognisable "LT" symbol.

lm.name: London  - Yellow hydrant with blue nozzle
lm.note: London's hydrants will almost always have blue nozzles.

lm.name: Mayo  - Vibes
lm.note:
Mayo can be recognised by a large forested hill to the South, the wooden street signs and the fully red fire hydrants marked by 3 red bollards. The town has a mix of Gen 2 and Gen 4 coverage.

Note: Wooden street signs can be found in multiple towns in the Yukon (eg. Haines Junction or Carmacks).

lm.name: Medicine Hat  - Bicolour traffic light
lm.note: Medicine Hat has some really stylish traffic lights with a yellow-black-yellow pattern. These are unique to the city.

lm.name: Medicine Hat  - Connection piece
lm.note: Street signs in Medicine Hat often have metal connection pieces between the sign and the post. They can be T-shape or U-shape.

lm.name: Medicine Hat  - Dry ridges
lm.note: Medicine has a distinctively dry landscape with many dry ridges in and around the city.

lm.name: Medicine Hat  - Green lamp
lm.note:
Medicine Hat uses a lot of green lamps. Surrounding cities often use brown.

Note: In some neighbourhoods the lamps can appear rusty.

lm.name: Medicine Hat / Lethbridge  - Red body hydrant
lm.note: Medicine Hat uses red body fire hydrants along with Lethbridge. While Medicine Hat uses white nozzles, Lethbridge uses black.

lm.name: Moncton  - Bell Aliant Tower
lm.note: The huge white Bell Aliant Tower is visible from most of Downtown Moncton. (Where you see blue street signs you will probably also see the tower.)

lm.name: Moncton  - Downtown logo
lm.note: Downtown Moncton uses a blue street sign with a city logo. The rest of the city uses the standard green signs with white lettering.

lm.name: Moncton  - Horizontal traffic light
lm.note: Moncton uses a horizontal traffic light with a black middle and a yellow frame. This is rare in New Brunswick.

lm.name: Moncton  - Red snow pole hydrant
lm.note: Moncton always has a red snowpole besides its fire hydrants.

lm.name: Montréal  - Black signback
lm.note: Montréal's inner city tends to use black backs of signs, lamps, signposts and other inftrastructure. Note: Other colours are possible.

lm.name: Montréal  - Brown compost bin
lm.note: These small brown compost bins are specific to Montréal. Note: Even if you can't see the city name on the front, you can recognise the bin by its colour and the unique trash circle logo.

lm.name: Montréal  - Chevron bus
lm.note: Montréal's buses have pretty distinctive "chevrons".

lm.name: Montréal  - Flower logo
lm.note: Montréal is easily identifiable thanks to the red flower logo on nearly all street signs. Street sign logos are a great way to identify cities in Québec.

lm.name: Montréal  - Red hydrant with yellow marker
lm.note: Red fire hydrants with yellow snowpoles are typical for Montréal.

lm.name: Montréal  - Vertical stoplight
lm.note: Downtown Montréal sometimes uses vertical stoplights which is an exception to the standard Québec style.

lm.name: Moose Jaw  - Green wooden lamppost
lm.note: Moose Jaw uses green painted wood for its lampposts. In some streets the paint can be quite faded.

lm.name: Moose Jaw  - MJTS bus stop
lm.note: Moose Jaw uses orange bus stop signs with an MJTS label.

lm.name: Moose Jaw  - Silver nozzles
lm.note: Fire hydrants in Moose Jaw are red with a silver top and silver nozzles.

lm.name: Mount Pearl  - Red-green hydrant
lm.note: Mount Pearl, just Southwest of St. John's has its own red fire hydrant design with a green top and nozzles.

lm.name: Mount Pearl / Torbay  - Arched street sign
lm.note: Mount Pearl and Torbay are both part of the St. John's Metropolitan area. They have similar metas to St. John's, except for their unique blue arched street signs. To tell them apart, you can look at what's inside the arch: Torbay has a logo with a bird and a wave and Mount Pearl has a crest surrounded by a "City of Mount Pearl" text.

lm.name: Nain  - Trekker coverage
lm.note:
Nain is the northernmost town with coverage in Labrador. It was covered by a trekker during some sort of an event. There are often groups of people walking around the camera.

Note: The pine trees and the rocky cliffs on the other side of the bay are also distinctive.

lm.name: Nanaimo  - White outline
lm.note:
The city of Nanaimo (which is on Vancouver Island) uses a thick white outline on a blue street sign + yellow curbs.

Note: This street sign is "T" shape as opposed to Victoria's "L" shape ones.

lm.name: Nelson  - Green signpost
lm.note: The city of Nelson uses distinct green signposts.

lm.name: Nelson  - Post-rain May
lm.note:
The typical coverage in Nelson has a humid, post-rain look with gray clouds and lush, vegetation covered mountains all around. The photos were taken in May 2025 with a Gen4 camera.

Note: The old Gen3 September coverage still exists, but it's mostly limited to the surrounding forest roads.

lm.name: Vertical traffic light
lm.note:
The standard Newfoundland & Labrador traffic light is vertical, yellow and has no frame. (This is only applicable to bigger towns.)

Note: The town of Gander is an exception with its black lights.

lm.name: Niagara Falls  - Blue Transit
lm.note: Niagara Falls uses blue bus stop signs and buses that are either fully white or white with a wave pattern on the front.

lm.name: Niagara Falls  - Fire route numbers
lm.note: Niagara Falls sometimes has fire route numbers on its street signs.

lm.name: Niagara Falls  - Octagonal lamppost
lm.note:
Suburban lampposts in Niagara Falls often use an octagonal concrete design.

Note: Lampposts are usually tagged with a yellow horizontal plate with numbers on it in a XX-XXX format.

lm.name: Nort West River / Sheshatshiu  - Landscape
lm.note: North West River and Sheshatshiu are found just North of Happy Valley. They look similar to Happy Valley, only hillier and located on a river.

lm.name: North West River  - Anniversary street sign
lm.note: North West River has its own street sign with an anniversary logo inside a semicircle on the top.

lm.name: Okanagan Valley  - Dryness
lm.note:
Kamloops, Kelowna and the whole Okanagan Valley is very dry, which looks pretty different to the rest of Canada. This region is very distinct and can look almost Mediterranean. Winyards and fruit plantations are a common sight here.

Note: Kamloops is located in the transition zone between the Okanagan and the wetter North so it can look somewhat greener than Kelowna.

lm.name: Ottawa  - Bent metal signpost
lm.note:
Ottawa signposts often use a single piece of bent metal, whereas the rest of Ontario prefers these dotted square signposts shown on the second image.

Note: Be careful, bent metal signposts can also have holes on them!

lm.name: Ottawa  - Bilingual signage
lm.note: Ottawa will almost always have bilingual signage due to its proximity and relation with Québec.

lm.name: Ottawa  - Blue cap hydrant
lm.note: Fire hydrants in Ottawa have a distinct blue cap on top, but are still the standard Ontario yellow.

lm.name: Ottawa  - Bus stop
lm.note: Ottawa's bus stop can be recognised by the red quarter "O" symbol in the top right corner.

lm.name: Ottawa  - Circular city logo
lm.note:
The Ottawa street sign can be recognised by the circular logo and the bilingualism. Blue street signs are rare in Ontario, most rural areas use green.

Note: Downtown Ottawa has some unique colour variantions, but the logo stays the same.

lm.name: Ottawa / Gatineau  - Car plate chaos
lm.note:
Because Ottawa is a connected city with Gatineau, main roads in these 2 cities will often have a mix of Ontario and Québec car plates. Only Ontario requires front plates.

Note: This is less common in residential areas.

lm.name: Conferederation Bridge
lm.note: This huge bridge with a lump in the middle is the Confederation Bridge connecting Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick.

lm.name: Pelly Crossing  - Vibes
lm.note: Pelly Crossing is a town located on the Klondike Highway. It has only highway coverage, mostly Gen 4 with the light blue Pelly River Bridge always in sight. Northern Tutchone, the traditional language of the Selkirk First Nation is featured on the street signs.

lm.name: Prince Albert  - Green signpost
lm.note:
Street sign posts in Prince Albert are often green.

Note: Their other common signpost is a thick, white wooden one which is used for holding street signs as well as traffic signs. You will often see both kind in the same intersecion.

lm.name: Prince Albert  - Red hydrant
lm.note:
Fire hydrants in Prince Albert are red.

Note: On the older Gen 3 coverage hydrants often had a blue top, but these have been faded or replaced by the time the Gen 4 photos were taken.

lm.name: Prince Albert  - Thick white signpost
lm.note:
Thick white wooden signposts are characteristic of Prince Albert.

Note: Thin green plastic signposts are also common there.

lm.name: Prince George  - Green lamp
lm.note: Prince George likes to use green lamps.

lm.name: Prince George  - Yellow hydrant
lm.note: Just like most cities in Central BC, Prince George uses fire hydrants with a yellow body. The top and the nozzles are usually red, but plain yellow hydrants are also fairly common.

lm.name: Qikiqtarjuak  - Vibes
lm.note:
Qikiqtarjuak is very mountainous. Other than Grise Fjord, it is the only town in Nunavut with mountains this large. Its reddish dirt is also distinct.

Note: The hazy Gen 3 with the red dirt makes this town very vibeable.

lm.name: Québec City  - Blue rectangle
lm.note: All hydrant markers in Québec City will use this blue rectangle on the side. This is a very reliable meta.

lm.name: Québec City  - European architecture
lm.note: The downtown part of Québec City is a tourist attraction because of its European architecture.

lm.name: Québec City  - RTC Buses
lm.note: Public transit in Québec City is operated by RTC (Reseau du Transport de la Capitale). Their buses are either lime green or dark blue, with a wide grey diagonal strip on the side.

lm.name: Québec City  - Street sign layout
lm.note: No logo on the street sign for Québec City, but the white background, the black text and the layout is memorable. Note: Many of these street signs will have a tiny font size for the kind of street (Rue, Avenue, etc.) and the cardinal directions and a much bigger font for the street name.

lm.name: Red Bay  - Vibes
lm.note:
Red Bay is a coastal town in Southern Labrador. It looks a bit like Nain, but the soil is redder and most of the houses are painted white. The weather is also gloomier.

Note: The lack of huge pine trees typical of Nain is also noteworthy.

lm.name: Red Deer  - Dark lamp
lm.note: Lamps painted dark are common in Red Deer. Neither Edmonton nor Calgary uses dark lamps.

lm.name: Red Deer  - Lime green hydrant
lm.note:
Red Deer has lime green fire hydrants with a row of numbers on top.

Note: While Calgary's hydrants have a similar green body, their nozzles are black.

lm.name: Red Deer  - Metal connection
lm.note: Red Deer has a lot of numbered streets and their street signs emphasize the numbers. The signs are usually connected horizontally with a small piece of metal on the pole side, but signs connected from below are also common.

lm.name: Red Deer  - Traffic light
lm.note:
Red Deer uses traffic lights with black lamps inside of a yellow frame. Edmonton's lights are fully black in the front and Calgary's are fully yellow.

Note: Red Deer is half way between Edmonton and Calgary - and so is the traffic light's colouring!

lm.name: Red Deer  - Yellow curbs
lm.note:
Yellow painted curbs and sewers are especially common in Red Deer, along with many rural Alberta towns.

Note: Yellow curbs show up in other parts of Canada too, so look for other clues first!

lm.name: Regina  - Blue street sign
lm.note: Regina is the only major city in Saskatchewan with blue street signs.

lm.name: Regina  - Horizontal street light
lm.note:
Traffic lights in Regina are fully yellow and horizontal. Saskatoon's are vertical.

Note: Horizontal traffic lights are not unique to Regina, they are pretty standard in Sask.

lm.name: Regina  - Regina Transit
lm.note: Regina Transit has a useful colour scheme: the blue and yellow stripes are visible on their buses and their bus stops as well.

lm.name: Regina  - Small holes signpost
lm.note: Regina and Saskatoon signposts are both rectangular with no holes. However, the lowest section on Regina's posts does feature some small holes. You can use this to differentiate between the two cities.

lm.name: Resolute  - Road to Airport
lm.note: The road to Resolute Bay Airport has a row of snow poles on the West side. A bit further behind them there is also a row of generic utility poles.

lm.name: Resolute  - Vibes
lm.note: Resolute can be recognised by the cloudy skies and the small ridge to the North with patchy snow. It feels like a less mountainous version of Qikiqtarjuak with Kyrgyzstan vibes.

lm.name: Ross River  - Vibes
lm.note:
Ross River has cloudy Gen 2 coverage with a distinct ridge to the North. Its street signs are the standard Yukon green with a white border. Yield signs are common in the town.

The gravel road leading into the town from the West has sunny Gen 4 coverage.

lm.name: Saguenay  - City logo
lm.note: Saguenay's city logo shows up on street signs and garbage bins in the city. The colour scheme is blue-white. Note: A simpler green sign with white letters and no logo is also possible to find.

lm.name: Saguenay  - Red hydrant, red marker
lm.note: Saguenay's hydrant markers match their hydrant's red colour. Some suburbs use this unique sketch-like drawing instead.

lm.name: Saint John  - Dark signpost
lm.note: Signposts in Saint John are often extremely rusty or dark.

lm.name: Saint John  - European vibe
lm.note: Downtown Saint John has a very unique European vibe.

lm.name: Saint John  - Grey nozzle hydrant
lm.note: Saint John uses red fire hydrants with a grey nozzle.

lm.name: Saint John  - Hills
lm.note: Saint John is hillier than other major cities in New Brunswick.

lm.name: Saint John  - Saint John Transit
lm.note: Saint John buses are white with a red and blue pattern on the front. Bus stops are orange and black.

lm.name: Sanikiluaq  - Vibes
lm.note: Coverage in Sanikiluaq can be identified by the snowmobiler wearing a dark brown coat. Sanikiluaq is easily confused with Inukjuak, a town in Northern Québec which has similar snowmobile coverage, but without the brown coat.

lm.name: Sarnia  - Orange bus stop
lm.note: Sarnia's bus stops are very noticeably orange. They can be seen from far away.

lm.name: Saskatoon  - Green street sign
lm.note: Saskatoon uses the standard green street signs with white lettering. Regina uses blue.

lm.name: Saskatoon  - Red top hydrant
lm.note: Saskatoon and Regina both use yellow body fire hydrants, however only Saskatoon has red tops on them.

lm.name: Saskatoon  - Saskatoon Transit
lm.note: Saskatoon Transit uses distinct blue shark-fin shaped bus stops and buses with a sky blue front.

lm.name: Saskatoon  - Vertical street light
lm.note: Saskatoon and Regina both use yellow traffic lights, but only Saskatoon's is vertical. This is quite rare in Saskatchewan.

lm.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - Black middle street light
lm.note: Street lights in Sault Ste. Marie are black in the middle.

lm.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - Red hydrant with blue top
lm.note: Sault Ste. Marie is one of the few cities in Ontario that use red fire hydrants. Below is the unique hydrant style with a blue top.

lm.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - White stripe street sign
lm.note: Sault Ste. Marie uses these unique blue street signs with white or metallic strips on the top and bottom.

lm.name: Sherbrooke  - Blue or green dot
lm.note: Sherbrooke's hydrant markers often have a blue or green dot inside one of the small rectangles. Otherwise they are pretty standard for Québec.

lm.name: Sherbrooke  - No Q pole sticker
lm.note: Sherbrooke and surrounding cities use a pole sticker without the usual Québec "black Q". The sticker will only have the vertical numbers and possibly some other letters on top.

lm.name: Sherbrooke  - Plain blue street sign
lm.note: Sherbrooke uses these minimalistic looking blue street signs. Note: On the 2011 coverage you might see their old green sign with a Sherbrooke logo. This coverage is extremely rare these days, so I wouldn't worry about it.

lm.name: Sherbrooke  - Wavy bin logo
lm.note: Sherbrooke garbage bins come with this very convenient city logo featuring the city's name riding a wave.

lm.name: Southwest BC Cities  - Sign clasps
lm.note:
Towns in South-West B.C. use thick metal sign clasps to attach their signs to the signpost.

Note: This includes the Vancouver Metro Area, Victoria and towns on the Sea-to-Sky Highway. For some reason, Nanaimo doesn't use them.

lm.name: St. John's  - Colourful houses
lm.note: St. John's is by far the largest city in Newfoundland & Labrador. The downtown area has many colourful houses.

lm.name: St. John's  - Torbay's arched street sign
lm.note: Mount Pearl and Torbay are both part of the St. John's Metropolitan area. They have similar metas to St. John's, except for their unique blue arched street signs. To tell them apart, you can look at what's inside the arch: Torbay has a logo with a bird and a wave and Mount Pearl has a crest surrounded by a "City of Mount Pearl" text.

lm.name: St. John's  - Yellow hydrant and diamond
lm.note:
Within Newfoundland, yellow fire hydrants and these skinny diamond snowpoles are unique to St. John's.

Note: The colour of the diamond may vary.

lm.name: Sudbury  - Mineral rocks
lm.note: Sudbury is a major mining hub located near the Sudbury Basin: an ancient meteorite impact crater. As a result, roads in the city are lined with walls of mineral-rich rocks. They look sharper and more colourful than the Canadian Shield protrusions found in other cities.

lm.name: Sudbury  - Standard street sign
lm.note:
Sudbury uses the Ontario standard from almost everything: metal signposts (Thunder bay uses wood), green street signs and yellow fire hydrants.

Note: While the hydrants are mostly pure yellow, dark coloured tops can also be found in the city.

lm.name: Sudbury  - Transit logos
lm.note: Sudbury has a variety of bus stop designs: one features a bus icon and the Sudbury logo, the other says "gova" in colourful letters. The buses are white and also have the "gova" logo.

lm.name: Sudbury  - Yellow pole marking
lm.note: Sudbury uses THICK yellow utility pole markings. They will always start with an "S" in Sudbury.

lm.name: Sudbury / Thunder Bay  - "Atlantic" sytle architecture
lm.note:
The architecture in Thunder Bay and Sudbury is different from Southern Ontario's. It resembles Atlantic Canada with more white siding material.

Note: Northern Ontario towns, such Kenora have similar architecture.

lm.name: Summerside  - Pole star
lm.note: Summerside has some pretty unique stars between the wires.

lm.name: Summerside  - Unique street sign
lm.note:
Summerside has unique blue street signs with a logo inside a semicircle and the town's name written underneath. The text is usually bilingual, which is less common in Charlottetown.

Note: The sign is often hanging from an ornate attachment piece.

lm.name: Summerside  - White nozzle hydrant
lm.note: Summerside uses red hydrants with a white nozzle, accompanied by a red snow pole. Charlottetown uses green or grey nozzles and no snowpole.

lm.name: Summerside  - Yellow pole sticker
lm.note:
Summerside always uses these yellow pole stickers, just like New Brunswick. The rest of Prince Edward Island uses the white horizontal sticker.

Note: The sticker often starts with an "S" in Summerside.

lm.name: Swift Current  - Black traffic light
lm.note:
Swift Current uses fully black traffic lights.

Note: Black traffic lights show up in Moose Jaw and occasionally in Estevan too. We could say it's a Southern Sask thing.

lm.name: Swift Current  - Blue nozzle hydrant
lm.note: Swift Current used to have a lot of red hydrants with a blue nozzle on the older Gen 3 coverage. On Gen 4, the nozzles can be other dark colours too, such as dark green or grey.

lm.name: Sydney  - "Western style" traffic light
lm.note:
Sydney uses a vertical yellow traffic light with a yellow frame which is common in Nova Scotia. Within Atlantic Canada, this design indicates NS.

Note 1: Some Western provinces (BC, SK, MB) use the same design, but the landscape is usually enough to tell them apart.

Note 2: If you see thin horizontal slots on the frame: those are specific to Nova Scotia.

lm.name: Sydney  - Secondary crossbeam
lm.note: Sydney and other major cities in Nova Scotia sometimes use secondary crossbeams.

lm.name: Sydney  - Transit Cape Breton
lm.note:
Sydney is the largest settlement on Cape Breton Island. The city's transit system is part of Transit Cape Breton whose name you will see on the city's buses. Bus stops say "CBRM - Cape Breton Regional Municipality".

Note: Even if you can't read the text, the green colour scheme is a good clue.

lm.name: Teslin  - Vibes
lm.note: Teslin is a town along the Alaska Highway. It has Gen 2 coverage only and a distinct hill to the Northwest. All lamps in Teslin have the same 2 flags.

lm.name: Thompson  - Overcast Gen2
lm.note: Thompson is basically the northernmost major town in Manitoba. It has only overcast Gen2 coverage with a red tinted halo in the sky.

lm.name: Thompson  - Pointy lamp
lm.note: Thompson uses a lot of this green lamp with a pointy top which is unique to Manitoba.

lm.name: Thunder Bay  - Bus stop
lm.note:
Thunder Bay bus stops can be identified by a bus icon inside a lime green circle.

Note: The sign also features the 807 area code.

lm.name: Thunder Bay  - Light yellow hydrants
lm.note:
Thunder Bay fire hydrants tend to be a lighter shade of yellow than the normal Ontario ones. The nozzles are also fully yellow, whereas most of Southern Ontario has coloured nozzles.

Note: Snow poles are optional.

lm.name: Thunder Bay  - Metal strip street sign
lm.note:
Street signs in Thunder Bay have a distinct design with a small strip of metal at the bottom with 2 screws. The post is square and wooden and has a recognisable shape.

Note: The metal strip can also be on the side of the sign.

lm.name: Thunder Bay  - Poor quality pavement
lm.note: To tell Thunder Bay apart from Sudbury: Thunder Bay is economically poorer and experiences cold Winters. As a result, cracks, potholes and tar snakes can often be seen on the pavement.

lm.name: Thunder Bay  - Ridge to the South
lm.note:
This large, distinct mountain is found to the South in Thunder Bay. It is the best way to recognise this city and is visible from many angles.

Note: The mountain might not be visible from the Northern half of the city.

lm.name: Timmins  - Number street sign
lm.note: On Timmins street signs you can see house numbers diplayed vertically on the two sides of the street name.

lm.name: Toronto  - CN Tower
lm.note: The CN Tower is the main landmark of Toronto and can be seen from surprisingly far away. Note: This is mostly true for the Downtown areas and Centre Island.

lm.name: Toronto  - Coloured nozzles
lm.note: Toronto uses the standard Ontario yellow hydrant. Sometimes it uses coloured nozzles to indicate water flow. (Often blue).

lm.name: Toronto  - Downtown Toronto lamp
lm.note: This lamp is specific to downtown Toronto.

lm.name: Toronto  - Garbage bin logo
lm.note: Most garbage bins in Toronto have a recognisable Toronto logo on them.

lm.name: Toronto  - Stripy street sign
lm.note: Within Toronto most street signs follow this unique stripy design. Note: The blue-white design has some interesting variations.

lm.name: Toronto  - Transit logo
lm.note:
Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) has a unique red logo that can be seen on bus and subway stops.

Note: The bus stop signs themselves are thin and have the same red and white colour scheme.

lm.name: Trois Riviéres  - Extra small hydrant marker
lm.note: Trois-Rivières uses an extra small yellow square to mark hydrants.

lm.name: Trois Riviéres  - White border street sign
lm.note: Trois-Rivières uses a green street sign with a thick white border.

lm.name: Tulita  - Vibes
lm.note: The brown dirt, the overcast skies and the short trees make Tulita easily recognisable. Sometimes you will see a white Google car with a bumper and an antenna on the right side. Sometimes only the antenna will be visible. For NMPZ: The main street has a unique poletop with 6 tiny insulators and a super short lamp.

lm.name: Val - 'd Or - Ordinal numbers
lm.note: Val-'d Or street signs can be green or white, but the layout of the ordinal numbers is pretty distinct.

lm.name: Val - 'd Or - Red-blue hydrant
lm.note: Val-'d Or uses these neat red fire hydrants with blue nozzles and a blue top.

lm.name: Vancouver  - Bus design
lm.note: Vancouver has a recognisable bus design: it's blue in the front and silver in the back.

lm.name: Vancouver area  - Common design hydrant
lm.note:
The most common fire hydrant design in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area features a red body and white nozzles.

Note: Vancouver City uses red nozzles and Burnaby has its own colour scheme.

lm.name: Vancouver Island  - Tall dense trees
lm.note:
Trees on Vancouver Island - including urban areas like Victoria and Nanaimo - are taller and denser. Parts of the island are a temperate rainforest.

Note: Giant hemlock trees are especially common here.

lm.name: Vancouver Island  - Yellow curbs
lm.note:
Vancouver Island likes to use more yellow curbs than Vancouver City.

Note: Be careful, yellow curbs can be found in other areas of Canada!

lm.name: Victoria  - "L" street sign
lm.note: Street signs in Victoria are mostly in an "L" shape.

lm.name: Victoria  - Green transit design
lm.note: Buses in Victoria have green stripes compared to Vancouver buses which have blue bottoms. Victoria also uses green stops, which can be either a regular square sign or a unique vertical design.

lm.name: Victoria  - White logo sign
lm.note:
The Township of Esquimalt, just West of Victoria uses its own street sign with the city's logo on it. This is not an "L" shape sign, like Victoria's.

Note: On the 2025 coverage the logo can be completely faded.

lm.name: Wabush  - Rain and street sign
lm.note:
Wabush, a town just South of Labrador City has only one road of coverage. This road can be identified by the rainy weather and the street signs with a red text.

Note: The clouds and the Sun being low on the horizon makes this coverage distinctly dark.

lm.name: Watson Lake  - Blue green lamp
lm.note: All Watson Lake locations on the Alaska Highway can be identified by these blue-green lamps. The lamps lining the main road are decorated with several flags.

lm.name: Watson Lake  - Sign Post Forest
lm.note: Watson Lake's "Sign Post Forest" is one of the most well-known landmarks along the Alaska Highway. It is situated at the intersection of the Alaska and the Robert Campbell Highways and is visible from the highlighted sections.

lm.name: Western BC towns  - Cloudy mountains
lm.note:
The Western cities are almost always identifiable due to their very cloudy, gray and mountainous coverage.

Note: While the weather conditions are more striking in Gen2, the clouds are visible on Gen4 as well.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Asymmetrical poletop
lm.note:
This poletop with an asymmetrical secondary crossbeam is especially common in and around Whitehorse.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Bin logo
lm.note:
The official logo of the City of Whitehorse can be found on the garbage bins. It features a steamboat with the city's name underneath.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Number hydrant
lm.note:
The typical Whitehorse fire hydrant is yellow and features black numbers on the front part.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Rocky ridges
lm.note:
Whitehorse is surrounded by large, sandy, light coloured ridges.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Rusted or replaced lamps
lm.note:
Lamps in Whitehorse are rusted, giving it a brown colour. Some neighbourhoods have freshly painted yellow or silver lamps.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Whitehorse  - Steamboat street sign
lm.note:
Street signs in Whitehorse are green and have a distinct steamboat logo on it, with "Whitehorse" written underneath.

Note 1: On the older Gen 2 coverage a white street sign with a green border can be seen instead. Note 2: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.

lm.name: Windsor  - Yellow hydrant with blue top
lm.note: Most of the fire hydrants in Windsor are yellow with a blue top.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - Go thru sign attachment
lm.note:
This type of sign attachment is unique to Winnipeg.

Note: 2 metal pieces pass through the sign from behind, so you can see 2 bolts on the front.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - Manitoba traffic light
lm.note: Winnipeg uses vertical yellow traffic lights. These are pretty standard for Manitoba. To differentiate between Manitoba and Ontario traffic lights, look at the top lamp: in Ontario it is bigger than the rest, in Manitoba it is the same size.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - Orange snow pole
lm.note:
Winnipeg usually has an orange snow pole beside the fire hydrant.

Note: Exceptions do exist.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - White pole sticker
lm.note:
Winnipeg uses large, white pole stickers with black numbers on some of its utility poles.

Note: These stickers are somewhat common in alleyways, but extremely rare elsewhere.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - White street sign
lm.note: Winnipeg street signs are always white.

lm.name: Winnipeg  - Winnipeg Transit
lm.note: Winnipeg buses are white with thin blue, yellow and red stripes on their side. Bus stops feature the "T" transit logo, in front of 3 diagonal stripes.

lm.name: Yarmouth  - Yellow body hydrant
lm.note: While most cities in Nova Scotia use red body fire hydrants, there are some notable yellow exceptions. Yarmouth has a yellow body hydrant with various top colours.

lm.name: Yellowknife  - Garbage bin
lm.note: Large wooden garbage bins of this specific shape are found in many driveways in Yellowknife. They can be painted in different colours.

lm.name: Yellowknife  - Green lamp
lm.note:
Green lamps are the main characteristic feature of Yellowknife. Whitehorse uses dark brown lamps.

Note: Yellowknife is Gen 2 only.

lm.name: Alberta License Plate
lm.note:
Alberta plates are white and have red on the left and right side.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: British Columbia license plate
lm.note:
British Columbia license plates are mostly white with green in the middle bottom.

Front plates required.

lm.name: Manitoba license plate
lm.note:
Manitoba license plates are white with green on the far left and right side. A small yellow part can often be seen too at the bottom.

Front plates required.

lm.name: New Brunswick license plate
lm.note:
New Brunswick license plates are white with red on the left and right side and a little bit of blue on the top which can be hard to spot.

NOTE: Since 2019, front plates are no longer required in New Brunswick. However, you should still expect to see them in older coverage. As well, all commercial vehicles in Newfoundland and Labrador are required to use front plates, and so it is possible to see them on vans and pickup trucks.

lm.name: Newfoundland and Labrador license plate
lm.note:
Newfoundland and Labrador license plates are white with blue on the left and right side. Sometimes it has square yellow and red parts in the bottom corners.

License plates in Labrador are very rare to see, pretty much only found in Happy Valley-Goose Bay. Churchill Falls and a few spots in Labrador City.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Northwest Territories plate
lm.note:
Northwest Territories plates have a cool polar bear shape, you can tell by the head sticking out on the top right.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Nova Scotia license plate
lm.note:
Nova Scotia license plates are white with blue in the middle and a little bit of blue around it sometimes.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Ontario license plate
lm.note:
Ontario license plates are most commonly white with blue on the left and right side.

Front plates required.

lm.name: Prince Edward Island license plate
lm.note:
Prince Edward Island license plates are either white with green in the middle and red in the left corner. Or just white with a bit of black and a smaller red part in the corners. Just check if it has those red corners and it should be a PEI plate.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Quebec license plate
lm.note:
Quebec license plates are white with blue on the left and right side, the blue is a bit darker than the blue Ontario and Nova Scotia use.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Saskatchewan license plate
lm.note:
Saskatchewan license plates are white with green on the left and right side, the plate can often look more green than white. Also sometimes also has a bit of orange in the middle.

Front plates not required.

lm.name: Yukon license plate
lm.note:
Yukon license plates are white with blue on the bottom left and right side with red between the blue. Also has a bit of orange on the left side.

Front plates not required.

top.html:
Canada uses the word ‘maximum’ on speed signs. Because speed is measured in kilometres instead of miles, the numbers tend to be higher than the US which can be identifiable from afar.

NOTE: The US uses the words ‘speed limit’ on such signs. In addition, speed limits ending with 5 are more common in the US, and the ‘speed limit’ text takes up two lines versus one for ‘maximum’ in Canada.
top.raw: Canada uses the word **‘maximum’ **on speed signs. Because speed is measured in kilometres instead of miles, the numbers tend to be higher than the US which can be identifiable from afar. NOTE: The US uses the words **‘speed limit’ **on such signs. In addition, speed limits ending with 5 are more common in the US, and the ‘speed limit’ text takes up two lines versus one for ‘maximum’ in Canada.

top.html: Canadian road signs tend to be less wordy compared to their US counterparts. Good examples of this are railroad crossing and yield signs. In the US, these usually have the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ and ‘yield’ written on them, whereas in Canada, these signs are typically blank.
top.raw: Canadian road signs tend to be **less wordy** compared to their US counterparts. Good examples of this are railroad crossing and yield signs. In the US, these usually have the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ and ‘yield’ written on them, whereas in Canada, these signs are typically** **blank.

top.html:
The English-speaking parts of Canada use British English spelling (e.g. centre; colour). In addition, Canada mostly uses the metric system. For example, speed is measured in kilometres per hour.

NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the US, where American English spelling and (usually) the imperial system are used. For example, the US measures speed in miles.
top.raw: The English-speaking parts of Canada use **British English** spelling (e.g. centre; colour). In addition, Canada mostly uses the [metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system). For example, speed is measured in **kilometres **per hour. NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the US, where American English spelling and (usually) the [imperial system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units) are used. For example, the US measures speed in miles.

top.html:
Canada uses unique diamond-shaped T-Intersection signs.

NOTE: Canada is the only country in the world where you can find these signs. The US, for example, uses rectangular T-Intersection signs.
top.raw: Canada uses unique **diamond**-shaped T-Intersection signs. NOTE: Canada is the only country in the world where you can find these signs. The US, for example, uses rectangular** **T-Intersection signs.

top.html:
Canadian roads usually have single yellow centre lines. However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common.

NOTE: Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US. This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.
top.raw: Canadian roads usually have **single yellow **centre lines. However, double middle yellow centre lines are still decently common. NOTE: Double yellow centre lines are more common in the US. This is not a 100% reliable clue, so make sure to use this along with other clues.

top.html:
Canada has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, especially in rural or remote areas. Generation 2 can be recognized by the big circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

NOTE: Generation 2 is very rare in the US. If you are between Canada and the US, and the location is in Generation 2, you are much more likely to be in Canada.

If you are between Canada and the US, and the location is in Generation 2, you are much more likely to be in Canada.

top.html:
Generation 3 is significantly more common in Canada than in the US.

In addition, the side mirrors are blurred out differently: While they generally appear as two peaks in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a single peak in the US.
top.raw: **Generation 3** is significantly more common in Canada than in the US. In addition, the side mirrors are blurred out differently: While they generally appear as **two peaks** in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a single peak in the US.

top.html:
You can sometimes find communal mailboxes in Canada. Personal mailboxes are still very common, though.

Canada Post has a red logo, which sometimes appears on mailboxes.

NOTE: These communal mailboxes are very rare in the US. In addition, the US Postal Service has a blue logo.
top.raw: You can sometimes find **communal mailboxes** in Canada. Personal mailboxes are still very common, though. Canada Post has a **red logo**, which sometimes appears on mailboxes. NOTE: These communal mailboxes are very rare in the US. In addition, the US Postal Service has a blue logo.

top.html: This style of mailbox, resting on top of a post and with a small flag on the side, is mostly associated with North America.
top.raw: This style of mailbox, resting on top of a post and with a **small flag** on the side, is mostly associated with North America.

top.html:
North America primarily uses wooden utility poles.

Several European countries also primarily use wooden utility poles. However, a concrete pole in particular is mostly associated with Europe.

In addition, the US and Canada use transformers that are large metallic cylinders. This will never be seen in European countries.
top.raw: North America primarily uses **wooden utility poles**.  Several European countries also primarily use wooden utility poles. However, a concrete pole in particular is mostly associated with Europe. In addition, the US and Canada use transformers that are **large metallic cylinders**. This will never be seen in European countries.

top.html: This style of insulator, which is raised slightly on top of the utility pole, can be a good clue for the US and Canada. It is not typically found in Europe. It is especially apparent on simple poles with a single insulator.

top.html:
The United States and Canada will usually have short license plates. Europe usually uses a long license plate which will also have a blue strip on the side.

NOTE: Each province has its own designs. An overview of the specific designs in each province can be seen in step 2.
